speechtext:

Business of the House

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER NOVEMBER 26   WEDNESDAY SITTINGS AS ON OTHER DAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a few words to this motion, which has given me considerable thought since I first saw it yesterday in Votes and Proceedings. I am well aware there are certain rules in the House of Commons. Although I am far from being an expert on the rules, I distinctly remember two of them. One is that one may not impute motives, and the other has to do with unparliamentary language. Therefore I find myself this morning under a most strict limitation in what I am about to say.
' No rule, of course, can stop any hon. member from thinking. People are not put in jail or otherwise punished for that, yet, in the Dominion of Canada. In thinking about this matter, it occurred to me there might be a coloured gentleman in the winter kindling, if he did not occupy the whole woodpile. Considering the strain under which I am working, that is the most I am permitted to say at this time if I do not wish to commit a breach of the first rule which I mentioned.
As to the second rule, my position is even worse. I will admit my thinking was clothed in language which was extremely unparliamentary. So unparliamentary was it, sir, that I found that with almost every second breath I was calling myself to order. I did not get the obedience that you always get when you use that word. So bad did things become, Mr. Speaker, that I had to use another of your prerogatives: I had to name myself. I know when a person is named in the House of Commons it must be a matter of some shame to him. Then I felt that the house had probably acted in the matter, and upon the appropriate motion I am going to assume that I have been expelled from this house for one day certain, which is tomorrow, the 26th of November.
My shame hanging so heavily upon me, I felt I must get away from Ottawa. I did not think I could take the stares which I would get from hon. members. After all, I like my friends to speak to me, and I thought perhaps I would lose even that favourable consideration. Therefore I have decided to shake the dust-or snow-of Ottawa from my feet and go to the city of Toronto. There I am sure I will meet many of my constituents. I am also quite sure they will forgive me. They might even go further than forgiving me. They might even join me in that well-known cry, "Come on, Stampeders!"

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER NOVEMBER 26   WEDNESDAY SITTINGS AS ON OTHER DAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I am going to say will be far less effective than what the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) has just said in his humorous manner. While I think most of us recognize the desire of the government

and of hon. members generally to facilitate the business of the house, I think the resolution now before us asks too much of us.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER NOVEMBER 26   WEDNESDAY SITTINGS AS ON OTHER DAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER NOVEMBER 26   WEDNESDAY SITTINGS AS ON OTHER DAYS
speechtext:
To sit day after day from eleven in the morning until eleven at night is a strain on all members. We not only have to attend the sittings of the house and meetings of committees; there is also a certain amount of correspondence to be dealt with, and preparation to be made for the business of the house. I think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is asking too much of the house. Personally I believe-and I know my colleagues agree with this-that in order to facilitate the business of the house some Saturday sittings are unavoidable and warranted at this time. New business is still being placed on the order paper. I suggest to the Prime Minister that he meet the private members of the house part way, and at least have no Saturday night sittings. Members of the house want to get home to their families for the week end. I do not criticize members of the house who will not remain here, but if we sit on Saturdays it means that, with few exceptions, the only members of the house who will attend will be those who come from the far east and the far west. That has been the experience, and it is frequently so even on Fridays. I suggest to the Prime Minister that he modify the motion now before the house and avoid Saturday night sittings.
There is one other point I want to make. If the Prime Minister does not meet the wishes of some members of the house for whom I am speaking, at least- this could be done. The motion reads, as on previous occasions of the kind, that the order of business and procedure on Saturdays shall be the same as on Fridays, which means that the hour from eight to nine is reserved for private bills. I do not believe that should be done. I say that, not because I am opposed to any of the private bills-although I am-but because I think if we are asked to sit on Saturday nights we should not make way for private bills when we are really sitting -to deal with the public business. I ask the Prime Minister, on behalf of a number of members of the house, not only those of my own party, to modify the proposal and not insist on Saturday night sittings.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER NOVEMBER 26   WEDNESDAY SITTINGS AS ON OTHER DAYS
speechtext: I should like to say a word. I shall confine my remarks about this resolution to the hour between eight and nine tonight. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, they will be to the point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER NOVEMBER 26   WEDNESDAY SITTINGS AS ON OTHER DAYS

Mr. Speaker, I trust hon. members will not feel there is any desire to

have divergent views on this subject between the government and private members. This motion is in the form in which it is usually proposed when it is hoped that parliament is nearing the end of the session. There is no desire on the part of the government to impose its will upon the membership of the house. A large number of members spend the week end in Ottawa. I know that they, like many other members of the house, are anxious to have due consideration given to all the business that has to be completed, but they hope that it may be dealt with in a proper manner without the session extending too far into the month of December.
If it is agreeable to the house to allow the motion to pass, and it seems to be the feeling of a majority of the members that without sitting on Saturday evening the business of the house can be expeditiously dealt with,
I am sure the Minister of Public Works will be glad to move at six o'clock tomorrow night that the house then adjourn and resume at eleven o'clock on Monday morning.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADIAN-OWNED TONNAGE IN STERLING FREIGHT CARGOES    ACCIDENT TO S.S. "CHELOHSIN"

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADIAN-OWNED TONNAGE IN STERLING FREIGHT CARGOES    ACCIDENT TO S.S. "CHELOHSIN"
speechtext:
On November 23 I asked a question about reports that an agreement on merchant shipping was being negotiated in Ottawa between the United Kingdom and Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said he would look into the matter and make a reply later. Can the Minister of Transport make a statement today in this connection?
On November 21 I asked a question about the wreck of the steamship Chelohsin which took place on the shores of Stanley park in Vancouver. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said he would look into that matter also, to ascertain whether or not there would be an investigation.

subtopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADIAN-OWNED TONNAGE IN STERLING FREIGHT CARGOES    ACCIDENT TO S.S. "CHELOHSIN"
speechtext:
With reference to the last question, as to the wreck of the S.S. Chelohsin, I have not yet received a report from the registrar of shipping at Vancouver, but I have ordered a preliminary investigation, as is usual in these cases. I shall be glad to advise my hon. friend of the result of that investigation when it is forthcoming.
Inquiries of the Ministry Dealing with the other question, I should like to say that conversations have taken place between Sir Gilmour Jenkins, permanent secretary of the British Ministry of Transport, and Mr. Clyne, chairman of the Canadian maritime commission, in regard to lack of cargoes available to Canadian flag shipping. The difficulty which Canadian flag vessels have always faced is that they are unable to accept cargoes where the freight is payable in sterling because Canadians must have dollars to pay expenses. Canadians are debarred for all practical purposes from the carriage of ECA cargoes because by act of congress 50 per cent of such cargoes must be carried in U.S. bottoms and the remainder are carried by ships of the recipient nations, of which Canada is not one.
Outside of ECA cargoes, dollar freights are becoming more and more scarce. The problem is not a new one, but has been accentuated by the fall in the freight market consequent upon devaluation. Last year an arrangement was made between the British Ministry of Transport and the Canadian maritime commission whereby the United Kingdom agreed to provide what were in effect dollar freights to Canadian flag vessels, whose owners were members of conference lines, upon the basis of division of cargoes on a conference basis.
In addition the United Kingdom agreed to provide convertible sterling for 45,000 tons per month for tramp tonnage. The conversations between British and Canadian shipping experts have not been concluded, but the object of such conversations is to reach an agreed basis of participation of Canadian-owned tonnage in sterling freight cargoes in face of present day conditions.

subtopic: BRIEF TO ROYAL COMMISSION ON ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES-QUESTION AS TO GOVERNMENT POLICY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: BRIEF TO ROYAL COMMISSION ON ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES-QUESTION AS TO GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
I have now had an opportunity, Mr. Speaker, of looking at press reports to which the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) referred in asking his question yesterday. On the basis of this question and a further question asked by the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), the issue seems to be this: Why, since the chairman of the national film board is a member of the government, was the brief presented by the board not a statement of government policy?


My answer is this: A brief was prepared and submitted to the members of the board. No adverse criticisms were registered by the board, three members of which are from outside the government service, and it was my understanding that the board concurred in the brief. As chairman of the board I explained that I did not agree with everything in the brief, and that, as a member of the government, I could not, therefore, commit the government to anything it contained. I added that, as the brief was intended for presentation to a royal commission which was expected to make an independent finding, I felt that the commission was entitled to hear views from all quarters. I said that I would not object to the brief being presented to the Massey commission, provided that it was clearly indicated to the commission that it did not represent government policy. I am informed by the chairman of the Massey commission that this view was made clear by the commissioner of the film board when the brief was presented.
In taking that attitude, I felt I was taking a liberal view while reserving the right of the government to formulate its own policies in the light of whatever recommendations might be made by the Massey commission.

I returned to my office this morning, and I understand that yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) raised the question of unemployment in the Vancouver area. It is true that since last summer some communications from labour and veterans organizations have been received in connection with the development of an unemployment situation in that area. I have directed my officers in the area to keep close watch on the situation, and to consult with interested organizations.
Recently I was in Vancouver, and while the situation does not appear to be as buoyant as it was a year ago, it can be said there is a high level of employment in that area. There are exceptional cases, but at the 45781-142
Combines Investigation Act moment the seasonal drop in employment has been taken care of by the agency which was created for the purpose, the unemployment insurance office. As my hon. friend knows- but I think it is well to repeat it-British Columbia, and particularly the Vancouver -Victoria area, is flooded by people moving from eastern Canada. Since 1941 the population of British Columbia has increased 36 per cent, and the total employment in British Columbia has increased 16 per cent since 1946, which is the highest figure for any province in the dominion.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, November 24, consideration in committee of Bill No. 144, to amend the Combines Investigation Act-Mr. Garson-Mr. Dion in the chair.
On section 1-Attorney general of Canada may institute and conduct prosecutions.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Under this section there are a number of questions that I should like to ask the minister. I shall refer to the particular portions of section 10 of the present act that are applicable. It says that it shall be the duty of the commission to receive and register, and, subject to the provisions of this act, to deal with applications for investigations of alleged combines; to bring to the attention of the minister every such application; to compile information and make studies concerning the existence in Canada of monopolies; to supply any person on request with information as to this act, and generally do such things as are necessary in order to carry out the provisions of the act.
In 1946, with a view to strengthening this act, section 10A was passed, which provides that the commissioner may receive complaints respecting practices alleged to be offences under this act, and may communicate the complaint and such evidence, if any, in
support thereof to the attorney general of the

Combines Investigation Act province within which the offence is alleged to have been committed, or to the Attorney General of Canada. As was said yesterday by the leader of the opposition, the bill before the committee adds little or nothing to the enforcement of the act. The minister candidly admitted that that was so.
The questions I wish to ask concern enforcement under section 10; for if parliament passes these amendments it needs to be assured, in view of recent experience, that they will be properly and unerringly followed so that we shall not find ourselves in the position of slightly altering the words of a statute and still making the question of enforcement dependent upon the whim, desire or orders of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I should like to know how many investigations have been conducted by the commissioner since October, 1935, under the provisions of section 10. I should like to ascertain what has been done, if anything, to prosecute under the report made in 1945 by the commissioner in connection with the matter of international cartels. A report was brought before parliament and published in the regular way, but, so far as I know, no prosecution has ever been undertaken. Why? The minister contends that the publication of a report by the combines commissioner constitutes a challenge to prosecution.
My next question is: What industries have been investigated since 1946 by the commissioner under the powers contained in this section? Are there at present reports in course of preparation by the commissioner touching certain industries that have been investigated? According to the Financial Post, this week's issue, two or three industries have been investigated, and the reports are now in process of completion. In any of these industries were any promises made by the wartime prices and trade board or by any member of the government that their assistance in production during the days of war would be regarded as insulating them from legal jeopardy?
In regard to these prospective reports I ask the minister these questions: Will they be submitted to the cabinet before they are published? Have any portions of them already been submitted to the cabinet, and if so, under what authority? For there is no provision in the statute for submission to anyone by the commissioner under this section. I should like the minister to advise the committee whether these reports will be expurgated in any way by the cabinet or by any member of the cabinet. I might add that in 1948 the then minister of justice indicated that there was no authority in the minister or anyone else to alter the reports made under section 10.

My next question is: In how many cases since 1946, when this act was amended, have reports been forwarded by the commissioner or the Attorney General of Canada to the attorneys general of any of the provinces, and to what provinces?. Have any of the provinces failed to prosecute on any report indicating a combine in any of the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I think it would be better to say "have any of the provinces not prosecuted."

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister is right. Have any of the attorneys general not done so?
Then there is another matter. Provision for the report to be made by the commissioner under the provisions of section 10 is provided for under section 27, subsection 5. I read it once more merely for the purpose of founding the question:
Any report of the commissioner or of a special commissioner, other than an interim report . . . shall within fifteen days after its receipt by the minister be made public, unless the commissioner states in writing to the minister that he believes the public interest would be better served by withholding publication . . .
Having regard to all the storm and turmoil of recent days, and the difficulties in which the Minister of Justice finds himself by reason of the interference of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, it might be wondered why the minister did not take up with the commissioner the question of giving a certificate in writing to the minister that in the public interest this report should not be published. It would have been so easy, if the public interest demanded it, for the commissioner, when he delivered that report, to have done so, and the argument would have been over. There is no use in trying to amend a section unless the section as it now stands is being enforced. The minister admits that the amendment will not add to the powers with respect to prosecution.
I have listened with interest to the explanation of the minister about the McGregor report, and have endeavoured to follow him as carefully as I could, having regard to its length. During the period from January until October 22 was not a suggestion made to the commissioner at some time that instead of an addendum he could give a certificate that it was not in the public interest to publish the report? Was such a representation made to the commissioner? If so, when was the first occasion on which this was done? Was the Minister of Trade and Commerce present on any of the occasions when Mr. McGregor was present?

These are questions that have not been cleared up as yet. They are material in ascertaining whether or not section 10 as amended will in fact be carried into effect.
I await the minister's answer to these questions before proceeding.

report of the inquiry has not yet been received. It is not in draft form. I do not want to seem to be difficult in these things, but there is no use in any person trying to testify as to facts that he does not know. He cannot possibly be truthful about it.
There is an implication in this question which I think is unfair to the government, namely, that the ministers have been giving exemptions from the law. I have been trying my very best, apparently with great infirmity of language, to make my point clear-that so far as the flour report is concerned-that is the one we are discussing-it was not a matter of anybody giving any exemption or privilege to an industry or to the companies in that industry. As it would be in all instances, it was the case of an industry under the wartime prices and trade board carrying out regulations passed under the War Measures Act, orders made in proper form, calling upon the industry to do certain things which, were they done in time of peace by voluntary agreement, would perhaps constitute an offence under the Combines Investigation Act. By the express terms of the wartime prices and trade board regulations, orders of the board prevailed, in the event of conflict, over any other statute, including the Combines Investigation Act.
The immunity that my hon. friends speaks of is not an immunity which arises out of the promise of any minister or official; it is an immunity which arises out of the terms of the wartime prices and trade board regulations, passed pursuant to a statute enacted by this parliament. That is the law, whether it is stated to be so or not by any minister or by any official.

The point is that if any of these things which an industry is thus directed to do happens to be such as might be a contravention of the Combines Investigation Act if done by voluntary agreement, there is not and cannot be any liability under the Combines Investigation Act.

The test is not whether an industry is merely under the wartime prices and trade board regulations. The test is whether the regulations which are applicable to the industry call upon it to do things which might otherwise be offences under the Combines Investigation Act. The difference between the two cases, as I am advised by members of the wartime prices and trade board-and I consulted Mr. Gordon in this connection-is that in the case of the flour report there was that type of order- that is, the subsidy and profit-control arrangement; whereas in the case of the bread report, there was not. The prosecutions therefore can, we think, be successfully taken. We are so advised by Alberta counsel whom we consulted in the case of the bread report. In the case of the flour report, however, apart altogether from the propriety of prosecuting people for doing the things that you direct them to do under one government department, there is grave question whether it would be possible to make out a case at law.
In this connection I think I should point out something that has a good deal to do with the motives which have been imputed to the government, because we have been accused of being too charitable towards certain interests. I would point out to the hon. member for Assiniboia that several of these bakery companies whom we shall be prosecuting are partly or wholly owned by milling companies or are subsidiaries of milling companies.

speechtext:
No, they cannot go to jail, but that does not enter into the question whether or not they should be entitled to a jury. As a matter of fact if I were counsel for the defence in a combines case I should be very much inclined to hope that it was not before a jury. That has been the experience. I am going to quote a few references in a moment, because if you follow the combines cases you will find that counsel for the accused usually try to get away from a jury. One of the outstanding instances-and I do not want to refer to the case unless somebody insists-occurred in 1932. In 1932 one of the greatest combines cases ever fought in this country was tried. There were eighteen counsel for the defence, and about twenty more sitting behind them who could not practice before the bar in Canada. If there was one thing more than another that they wanted, it was to have a trial without a jury.
Some will say to me, as the minister did the other day in his general summary, that the proceedings in these cases take quite a while. If the combine has been detrimental to the public interest, the possibility of the case taking a few more days is scarcely an answer to the question whether or not juries should be done away with in combines cases.
A former attorney general of the United States, now a member of the supreme court of that country, tried on more than one occasion while he was attorney general to depart, ff it was possible to do so, from the constitutional provisions of the United States and to provide for trial before a judge without a jury. In the two minutes at my disposal before one o'clock I cannot quote him, but I shall do so after we resume.
In 1946 Mr. Ilsley said that the greatest deterrent was publicity. He advocated publication of the report, and said that the people as a whole know whether or not their rights are being interfered with. The attitude towards combines changes with the years. It becomes a matter of judicial interpretation. What was an offence thirty years ago may not, in the opinion of a judge, be an offence today. But a jury has that abiding sense of what public opinion is. I feel that taking away the jury in the trials of combines, and the like, is in fact removing one of the greatest and most positive sanctions in the preservation of law.
I cannot conceive that the excuse that it takes a little longer, that it is difficult for

Combines Investigation Act juries to understand-this was implied in words of the Minister of Justice-the complexity of some documents, is a good one for the departure from the jury system which I believe is peculiarly fitted to meet the demands of public opinion. Two years ago Mr. Ilsley said that this was the reason for publicity. He said: Give the people the story as to what the commissioner has found. Let them know. Let public opinion be aroused. Let it be created. Let the people realize what is taking place. I was one who took the stand, and was criticized for having done so, that we should not publish the report before the trial because it would interfere with the fairness of the trial. That was brushed aside. The point he made was this: public opinion must be created. Only by public opinion can laws such as the combines laws be maintained.
A judge, with all his learning, still does not have the infallibility that is created by public opinion. Twelve men on a jury trying a matter such as this know what fairness is and what exploitation is, as no judge, removed as he must be by his position from public opinion, can ever know. It is not just a question of law. The judge will instruct the jury on the law. If ever you want to see to it that the law is maintained and that public opinion enters into the maintenance of law, it is in the law of combines.

speechtext:
Not having occupied the position of judge and having little hope of ever being in that position, I find the question too hypothetical to answer. I had mentioned before lunch that the jury is indeed the conscience of the people in their attitude toward and interpretation in the light of the law of social problems. I mentioned what Mr. Ilsley had said in 1948 and I should like to quote that because it summarizes his view as to the need of publicity in connection with a report under section 27 (5). As reported on page 4919 of Hansard of June 8, 1948, Mr. Ilsley said:
I submit that it is necessary that there be publicity. At least, it is my contention or submission that there should be publicity. This offence is not at all like an offence that speaks for itself. It is all a mystery. The public has no way of knowing whether there is any combine or not. It is not like theft, bank robbery or any of those other overt or open acts where it is clear that there has been an offence. Here there is just a dark surmise and that is all. If the public is to know anything at all about this, it must be explained to them by the report of somebody who has made an investigation. If you have no provision that that report is to be made public,-
I accentuate these words:
-there is no possibility of an opportunity for public opinion to operate on governments, attorneys general or ministers of justice. There is no pos-

sibility of that; and you have to make a strong assumption that public officials will be fully alive to their responsibilities.
But after all, there is not much difference between the publication of a report by the commissioner and a preliminary inquiry into a criminal action. The commissioner has no judicial power; that is, he cannot himself determine the guilt of the accused. All he can do is express an opinion. The question is how far he should go in expressing an opinion, and whether he should not confine himself fairly well to facts.
I shall now summarize my submission in connection with this section. As I understand the Minister of Justice, one reason he advanced for not having juries in combine cases against companies is the complexity of the evidence, consisting as it must in considerable part of voluminous documents, memoranda and the like. Second, it would require a great deal of time for counsel who would have to read the documents. The minister cited the dental case as an example. He said there were 1,800 documents put in and that it took a long time to read them, and the whole case took some three weeks at the outside.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: And the crown lost the case.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, but the jury never got a chance, because no facts were placed before them upon which they could convict. I submit that expediency or shortening the period of trial should not weigh in the scales against having a jury.
Another argument was that corporations and not natural persons would be affected. A corporation is a natural person. When corporations are charged with conspiracy under British law or with an offence corresponding with that in section 498 of the Criminal Code, they have an inherent right to trial by jury. In the United States combines must be tried by jury because of the particular provisions of their constitution.
My first point is that no justification or excuse has been shown to abolish the time-honoured body whose responsibility is to determine the evidence. Throughout the years juries have upheld progress. The jury constitutes the public conscience. The jurors represent the community sense of justice. History and experience show that they have by their verdicts protected the individual against unjust and unfair laws. In other words, they have been the upholders of the collective conscience of the community.
Where is there a better type of case for a jury to try than a combines case? The attitude of the law changes over the years. The public conscience changes, and it has changed in regard to combines. There are two different views on the subject. There is the United States view that bigness of itself is an offence.
Combines Investigation Act The American attitude is that the size of a business determines in large degree whether or not it is a combine detrimental to the public. The British concept is that bigness of itself is insufficient to found a conviction, and that the detrimental effect on the community must be taken into consideration and proven.
The experience of the effects of big business has shown that a major reason why we have so high a standard of living is the mass production which has resulted from combinations in business that have been not detrimental to the public but actually beneficial to progress. The British concept is that there is detriment in agreements designed to destroy competition, and having destroyed competition they are detrimental to the public interest, in particular to the producer or the consumer. A reading of the authorities in the United States reveals a long record of trust-busting. Since the days of Theodore Roosevelt, there has been a changing attitude apparent in the United States Supreme Court decisions. That trend has finally arrived at a point where, under the recent anti-trust acts, a large corporation is, by reason of size, presumed to be dangerous to the public interest.
In Canada, following as we do the British attitude and concept, the whole basis of prosecution is dependent on proof by the prose-tion that what has been done will detrimentally affect the public interest, or is likely to do so. I believe that twelve good men and true, representing as they necessarily must different views, occupations, backgrounds and traditions, when operating in unison on a jury, will represent the public attitude more correctly in regard to alleged detrimental acts charged against a defendant than a judge without a jury. In making that statement no criticism is intended of any judge, or of the judiciary generally. In his position a judge is detached and above the influence of public opinion in the judgments that he renders. Holding that high and exalted position, he must necessarily be. The twelve jurymen are men of the world and men of the community. They know the public interest. I believe this question should be seriously considered before doing away with trial by jury in combines cases in so far as corporations are concerned. In my opinion, doing away with a jury is removing the effective deterrent of public opinion, upon the enforcement of which this legislation is dependent.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not objecting to the amendment as such, but I think the time has arrived in Canada when the Department of Justice and the departments of the attorneys general of the various provinces should move with extreme caution in doing away with the time-honoured system of jury trials. I did not have the privilege of hearing the opening remarks of the Minister of Justice on this section, but in the various provinces there is a system under our civil procedure whereby a judge can, on application, withdraw a case from a jury before trial. It is done because of the facts of the case. If they deal with questions of technique, questions of science, questions of immense calculations of figures, and so on, then if the judge is satisfied to that effect he can withdraw such a case from a jury and try it himself. In many cases the judge will then send for an assessor, or some official of that kind, to assess and calculate, where it is a matter of figures, so that the judge may come to a better conclusion upon such questions.
I have not much doubt that companies acting in restraint of trade would rather not have juries because usually juries are looked upon as being against big interests. On behalf of juries I want to say that I defended criminals in my own province and in one of the western provinces. I prosecuted for the attorney general's department for a good many years, and I was a member of the judiciary where I tried many criminal and civil cases. Only in one instance did it come to my attention that a jury did not arrive at a result which I considered satisfactory in the interests of justice and of everyone concerned. It was the first criminal case I ever defended in the province of Nova Scotia. The man was acquitted and he should have been convicted. He was acquitted, not because of any great intellectual address I made to the jury, or because of any great maxims of law that I presented to the judge and jury. After the trial the foreman told me the reason was that I was a newcomer in the community and not a bad sort of fellow and he said the jury thought they would give us a chance. Nevertheless, I am not convinced that is any reason for taking away from juries the right to try criminal offences.
I am not objecting to the adoption of this amendment. All I am suggesting is that the


justice department and the various provincial departments go very slow in doing away with the time-honoured right of citizens of this country, whether they be individuals or combinations of citizens in the form of companies, of being tried by a jury on any criminal charge. I am not sure whether or not it is in the Criminal Code, but in the province of Nova Scotia we have a provision under which the attorney general may request the judge in a particular case to send that case back to the district court for trial. Or perhaps it is the other way around and the attorney general has the right to intervene in order to prevent a person from going to trial before the district court.
At the moment we are dealing with a corporate entity, not an individual. I should think this is the sort of legislation that would be asked for by the big corporations, because generally speaking juries have the reputation of being against corporations. As far as my own province is concerned, I think the people there know pretty well where I stand in regard to combines in restraint of trade and particularly cartels. I am not speaking to this amendment because I think it will be unfair to any particular company that may be charged; but it seems to me that if a company is charged with a crime that flows from the ten commandments of God or from the natural law, it would have an absolute right to the privilege enjoyed by any individual in this country, of having the matter disposed of by a jury. They should not try to get away from that position; they should not ask for any special legislation. I am not suggesting that this amendment has resulted from anything said by any company or corporation in this country that may have been or in future may be charged under this section of the act. I would rather suspect that this has been suggested by the gentleman wh< has been prosecuting these cases, who has been finding it difficult to get juries to give judgments against those accused.
I should rather think that a corporation or combination of corporations charged under this act would have the right to go to a district court judge and elect speedy trial. If that is the case I do not see why it is necessary to bring in this amendment. I am not so sure on that point; it may be that only persons who are held in jail have that privilege, but I do know that in some cases, at least, companies charged with offences, though not under this legislation, have exercised that option and gone before a judge.
The Minister of Justice has given as the reason for this amendment the fact that in

these prosecutions so many intricate matters have to be dealt with that it is better to proceed without a jury. Even so, I believe the department should give consideration to permitting the judge presiding over a trial of this kind the privilege of exercising the prerogative which judges now possess in civil cases, that of taking the case away from the jury and trying it themselves if that course seems indicated. I have no doubt in the world that the present judges throughout this country-I am not referring to those who have been on the bench in the past-would exercise the very greatest care and caution to see that justice was done in these matters.
I had intended to say a word on the next amendment, but perhaps I had better wait until it is called.

Mr. Chairman, it is a bold thing for one who is not a lawyer to step into a debate that has been carried on by lawyers. As I have confessed to this house in times past, I am only a kind of reformed lawyer, but I should like to say just a word on this because I would hope that even at this late stage it might be possible to persuade the minister to have regard to what has been said by the last two speakers. It may be that juries sometimes make mistakes, but after all the electorate sometimes makes mistakes, too; and even those who feel that the electorate made a mistake do not suggest that the law should be changed to deprive it of its functions.
Speaking seriously, however, it seems to me important not only that the decision in any prosecution should be right, but that the public should accept it as right. In my opinion, there is unfortunately more danger of the public misunderstanding and not accepting a verdict when it is given by only one man who, as has been said already, may appear to the public to be somewhat remote from them, than if the decision were given by a jury. But the real reason I rose was not to express my own view but to present a bit of evidence from a man with vast experience with juries, and this is the last thing I want to say. I remember years ago reading a statement of the late Lord Birkenhead, who you will remember was first of all a great lawyer and finally lord chancellor. As I recall it he said that after trying hundreds of jury cases he thought the juries had been right in every case but three, and that in two of those three cases where he originally thought they had been wrong, subsequent knowledge and subsequent reflection had made him believe them to be right.
That is the view of a man who I suppose would have as much right to express an
Combines Investigation Act opinion on juries as any man in our generation. That is extraordinary praise, it seems to me, for this institution which you might say has become part of the pattern of our life. As the last speaker said, it seems to me a pity if, without the greatest and most profound consideration and even hesitation, this amendment should take away this time-honoured and effective institution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think perhaps the remarks that have been made require a short reply. I am in the rather paradoxical position of agreeing with all the reasons that the preceding speakers have advanced but differing completely from the conclusions they have reached. The reason I differ, I think, is that as I understood their remarks they mainly had to do with the ordinary run of jury cases in which the liberty of the subject is involved. In this case, so far as the withdrawal of the right to trial by jury is concerned, I believe every member of the house is agreed that there would be an overwhelming disposition to maintain trial by jury, which has been granted to people of British descent by Magna Carta and the Bill of Rights of 1689. That is not what we are really concerned with, however, in the Combines Investigation Act. The trying of a corporation by jury is not a time-honoured process by any means; it is a development that has taken place within the last one hundred years.
It requires but a slight amount of common sense to realize that a corporation cannot be tried by a jury of its peers. You cannot impanel a jury of twelve corporations to try a corporation. The real necessity for trying cases under the Combines Investigation Act by a judge alone, arises out of the consideration that was mentioned by the member for Inverness-Richmond when he said there is power now, in cases involving specialized knowledge, to withdraw the case from the jury and turn it over to an assessor or some officer of the crown.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Is that not only in civil cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, but the principle is the same. In any case, this is a statutory crime with which we are dealing, really a sort of economic offence.
The real point in connection with these charges under the Combines Investigation Act is that there may be a dozen companies indicted, and the charges may cover a multitude of facts extending over a long period of years. In studying the evidence that is presented, corporate interrelationships of an intricate nature are usually involved, with exhibits running into the hundreds. Then the length of time which a

Combines Investigation Act trial takes is considerable. In the Imperial Tobacco case in Alberta the trial lasted for 56 days. When you impanel a jury of busy people, and in my experience jurymen are always busy and are reluctant to be impanelled at all, and then ask them to absent themselves from business for 11 or 12 weeks in order to try the case, you can realize what a burden it imposes on the jury, and that you are not likely to maximize the disposition of the jury to dispense justice by insisting that the jury stay together for that length of time. It is due to these considerations that, not the large corporation, not the boards of trade, as the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond said, but those who are charged with the administration of this act have asked that the option which is now enjoyed by corporations of being tried with or without a jury be withdrawn.
As I did on a former occasion, I desire to emphasize that there is not the slightest suggestion that that option should be withdrawn from any individual accused.

Before the title carries, Mr. Speaker, I suggest there are two or three respects in which this act is still very weak, and I should like to call the attention of the house to a few particulars in which we think the act needs strengthening. In order to place my views before the house I shall move an amendment, which I believe it is competent to do before the title carries. In order that I may place the amendment before the Chair, I shall read it and then comment upon it. Of necessity, it is rather long but that cannot be avoided.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis):
That the bill be amended by adding thereto a new section 4, as follows:
4. The said act is further amended by adding the following section immediately after section 31 thereof:
31 A. (1) Whenever, from or as a result of an investigation under the provisions of this act, or from or as a result of a judgment of the supreme court or exchequer court of Canada or of any superior court, or circuit, district or county court in Canada, it appears to the satisfaction of the governor in council that a combine exists, the governor in council may issue and cause to be served on any person, an order requiring him to cease or desist from such acts or practices actually

proved against him and which in whole or in part constitute the operations of a combine or the processes of the formation of such, and to cease and desist as well from any other act or practice in pursuance of the operations of such combine or the formation thereof, to the extent to which the governor in council shall deem it reasonable or necessary to prohibit.
(2) Any person whom the governor in council shall have so ordered to cease or desist from any act or practice in pursuance of the operations of a combine or the formation thereof, and who thereafter shall omit or refuse to desist from such act or practice, shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding one thousand dollars and costs for each day after the expiration of ten days or such further extension of time as in the opinion of the governor in council may be reasonable or necessary, from the date of the service upon such person of the order, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years; and any director or officer of a company or corporation who shall assent to or acquiesce in such omission or refusal by his company or corporation shall be guilty of such offence personally, and cumulatively with his company or corporation and with his co-directors or associate officers.
While it has been placed in legal form, which I am advised is the proper form in which the amendment should be placed, it has a very simple meaning. It means that the governor in council may call upon any corporation or any individual against whom proof exists that they have formed a combination to restrict competition, or to obtain a common price level, or have done other acts which bring them within the scope of the Combines Investigation Act, to cease or desist even before the case goes before the law courts. I understand that such a provision was in the original act, and it is necessary that the government should have this power today. I believe it is in the public interest that an amendment of this sort should be placed in the act. I believe I am within my rights in moving such an amendment now.
Although couched in legal phraseology, and in rather more lengthy terms than I like placing before the house, the meaning of the amendment is quite clear. It is that the governor general shall have the power under this act to call upon corporations, individuals or groups who may be involved in a pricefixing or other combination, to cease and desist from acting as a combination, the one with the other.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this is a proper amendment to move at this time. The act is under our consideration, and apparently we are all in favour of reinforcing it in every particular in which it can be strengthened. Under the rules of this house and the citations in our books of rules and order, I think it is quite in order to move this amendment at this time; and I therefore move it.

One is rather reluctant, Mr. Chairman, to embark upon a discussion of a motion of this sort which apparently has had a great deal of thought upon the part of the hon. gentleman who moved it, especially without any advance notice of its contents and without any opportunity of preparing to meet it. But I would suggest, from the casual reading of this amendment that I have had the opportunity to do, that it is inadvisable for us to pass it. What is more, I am seriously of the opinion that it is ultra vires of this parliament to pass. The cease and desist order which my hon. friend has in mind is, as I understand it, a prominent feature of the United States method of dealing with combines and monopolies. But the method which is used in that country is conceived
Combines Investigation Act on quite a different basis from the basis of our act. Apart altogether from any question as to whether it is within the power of this parliament to enact-and speaking offhand as I must-it would seem to me that our act would have to be examined in an over-all way in order to accommodate the act as a whole for the insertion into it of this remedy; because a remedy such as this that is granted by any statute does not stand out naked and stark by itself; it is usually associated with a number of other sections which give it support and meaning. On that ground, I think it would be highly inadvisable for this committee to pass this present amendment, on grounds of substance.
But apart from that, when my hon. friend says that this was in the original act, I am wondering if he has not in mind the Board of Commerce Act, 1919, and that this section he is here advocating was a section of that Board of Commerce Act, which, it is true, was enacted as a supplement to our Combines Investigation Act; but it was a supplement with a most unhappy history. The Board of Commerce Act, having been passed by this parliament, was taken to the privy council and was there declared ultra vires. One must bear in mind the fact that our own Combines Investigation Act, upon being taken to the privy council, was debated at great length by competent lawyers; one of them told me that so far as he could judge two of the five judges of the privy council who heard the case seemed in favour of one side, and two seemed in favour of another, while the fifth did not commit himself at all. After a long period of reservation of judgment, the judgment came down upholding the validity of the Combines Investigation Act.
If we were to introduce into this bill any provision such as the one my hon. friend has moved and which is, at the very least, much similar to that of the Board of Commerce Act, I apprehend that it would not only be ultra vires of this parliament to deal with the section that my hon. friend has moved, but that if we were to attach it to the Combines Investigation Act, we would run grave danger of having the whole Combines Investigation Act declared ultra vires. For these reasons I think the committee should not entertain the motion.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief because I realize we have had an extended debate on this bill and I wish to thank the house for its courtesy. I should like to move:
That the bill be amended by adding thereto a new section 4, as follows:
"4. Subsection one of section two of the said act is amended by inserting after the word 'commodity' in line two thereof, the words 'or to any service,' and by adding at the end of paragraph (c) thereof the words 'a common or fixed charge for a service or'."
I think there is a weakness in this act because there are certain services of which we have knowledge which cannot be dealt with at the present time. For example, I have seen a radio broadcasting price list covering certain services to be rendered by private stations from one end of this country to the other and quoting exactly the same prices for exactly the same services. I have photographic copies of such lists which contain instructions that the prices listed are to be charged for certain services. If the radio committee had met at this session I intended to bring copies of the price lists issued by the

Canadian Association of Broadcasters to the attention of that committee. These are comprehensive lists of charges which the members of the association must observe. That is a combination in restraint of competition in connection with radio broadcasting fees, yet nothing can be done about it under this act.
I should like to give just one more example. The hon. member for Kamloops has raised the question of crime comics. I do not know whether a news vendor's activities would be considered as a service, but I have been reliably informed that these news vendors enter into agreements with agencies to accept an assortment of publications, such assortment containing such things as crime comics. The other day I spoke to a news vendor who is opposed to crime comics and asked her why she had them on her shelves. She told me that she could not help it because she had to take the assortment. Whether that can be regarded as a service or a commodity I am not sure and I do not propose to enter into a legal argument with the Minister of Justice or anybody else regarding that point.
There are other activities which fall into the category of services that are not covered by this act, but I do not intend to deal with them at the moment. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister now by moving this amendment.

speechtext:
Of course that would do away with the necessity for a lengthy discussion at this stage. I hope the minister will arrange to have some official of the Temiscouata Railway Company called before the standing committee, and also some officer or officers of the Canadian National Railways. In his

statement on the resolution stage the minister intimated that Canadian National Railways would be making quite substantial capital expenditures. I think it would be beneficial to have officials of that company called before the standing committee.
I also suggest that the position of the Canadian National Railways in connection with this railway should be made clear and kept clear. It is perfectly obvious that they are being placed in an unfair position. The minister explained that Canadian National Railways had been requested to take over the Temiscouata railway and had declined to do so, but eventually had been instructed by the government to take over that line. As I said a moment ago, it is obvious that they are going to have to make substantial capital expenditures, and that there will be a large increase in the wage bill. I think the minister gave the increase in wages as $140,000, which would amount to an increase of 54 per cent over the wages being paid at the present time. By that increase alone any small profit made by the company would be completely wiped out, and as a matter of fact in 1948 there was a small deficit.
So it is perfectly clear that this railway is going to be a losing proposition for the Canadian National. There may be justification for having the line taken over, but it could only be on the basis of a public service to the people of the district. If that service is to be rendered by the Canadian National that company should not be expected to show any profit as a result of the transaction. During the previous discussion we suggested to the minister that it might be possible to keep the accounts of railways such as this, which the Canadian National is forced to take over, separate from other accounts. I would hope that some such method could be adopted, because obviously it is unfair to expect the Canadian National Railways to show that they are carrying on a businesslike operation when they are forced to take over a railway which is losing money, as the Temiscouata railway is bound to do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE BY GOVERNMENT OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was surprised at the remarks just made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I admit that this railway is outside British Columbia, but it serves a great purpose and is a national asset. My hon. friend has enough experience and is enough of a businessman to realize that a railway which has survived for sixty years deserves special consideration. It helps the people of my county, and everyone is asking that this action be taken. The company has made great sacrifices to maintain the service for the benefit of the people, but since the

mares were subscribed but not paid for in the first instance the company has run into debt because of the interest that had to be paid on loans. But it has done splendidly, and I must congratulate the management and personnel of the company who have done very well.
The other day the hon. member for Vic-toria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) said he was in favour of the proposal. He has a great advantage over the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra, because he is familiar with the situation. Here we have on the one hand an hon. member who lives just across the river and who knows the railway line as well as he knows his own desk in this house, while on the other hand we have an hon. gentleman who lives thousands of miles away, who has never seen the railway or the country. He takes his magnifying glass and finds some objection to the purchase of that line. Where is Canadian unity in that? When did my hon. friend hear me speak against any proposed expenditures in the province of British Columbia? I have never complained about the millions of dollars that have been spent in his province. I considered British Columbia part of Canada, and that we should be prepared to help it.
Here we have a public service being given the electors of Temiscouata and Madawaska counties, and the hon. gentleman pulls out his magnifying glass and his telescope and says, "Well, we must be very careful about it; it may interfere with the Canadian National Railways." It will interfere very much with the people of Temiscouata and Madawaska if the Canadian National is interfered with in its intention to take over the railway.
That is that. I regret what my hon. friend has said.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE BY GOVERNMENT OF CANADA
speechtext: Then this was all cooked up ahead of time?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE BY GOVERNMENT OF CANADA
speechtext:
I shall repeat the words of the Prime Minister, because I wish to thank him personally; the other day, when he was not in the house, I conveyed my thanks through Hansard. I report the incident faithfully. When I asked what about the railway he replied, "Oh, yes". Then he mentioned my name and mentioned that I was like St. Thomas, that 1 could not believe without seeing, but that my constituents could be sure of him and could believe without seeing, which is much better. There were loud cheers and the the people were very happy, because he announced that the government would do precisely what is being done now.
If it were not a matter of public interest I would not insist upon it. I know the hardships and difficulties that have been experienced by the management in attempting to run the railway. These difficulties were caused by the lack of money to put the railroad in good condition so that it could become prosperous. One cannot judge the importance of the railway by the amount of last year's revenue. Some important improvements are necessary, and I am sure the Canadian National will make a good job of running the Temiscouata railway. Probably before the end of the year it will again be a paying proposition. In the meantime, it will serve the interests of the Canadian National as well as the population of the counties of Madawaska and Temiscouata.
There is another essential consideration, anu that is that the Temiscouata railway is the most easterly link between the transcontinental line and the Intercolonial railway, both operated by the Canadian National. It will help the transcontinental section as well

Temiscouata Railway
as the Intercolonial to have the Temiscouata serving as the hyphen between them. I am sorry that I have not a large map of the counties of Madawaska and Temiscouata to hang under the clock to show the line to the members of the house. Although this railway line is not located in the province of British Columbia, I expect I can rely on the support of my hon. friend from that province. Immediately following this, there is a bill for a railway in British Columbia, and in order to avoid obstruction I suggest that we pair them.
The government is doing quite well for British Columbia, as it is for Temiscouata. I again convey my thanks to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport and the officials of the Canadian National Railways. I wish to express my gratitude to the management of the Temiscouata railway and to Mr. Charles Stewart, the father of Bill Stewart of the Canadian Press, a man who has done so much for the railway. I wish to extend my thanks also to Mr. Tom Walsh, Mr. L. N. Ouellet and many others who have sacrificed so much in accepting a rate of pay which was about one-half the regular rate for railway employees who belong to the unions.
It is important also to remember that the Canadian National Railways' management has studied the case. Mr. Fairweather is familiar with it, and the officials have recommended the purchase of the Temiscouata railway by the Canadian National. This would have been accomplished during the days of Sir Henry Thornton if the Temiscouata had not been under the control of the Quebec Central Railway, which was owned by the C. P. R. at that time. The Temiscouata railway was never owned by the C. P. R., but at one time the directors of the Temiscouata were gentlemen who were also directors of the Quebec Central, a subsidiary of the C. P. R. This was the only reason for not amalgamating the Temiscouata railway with the Canadian National at the time the Gaspe railway and other railways in the province of Quebec were taken over, and that was about twenty years ago.
There were many difficulties in the way of improving the service. When Mr. Michaud was the member for Madawaska he knew the situation well, and these directors were replaced by men who lived at Edmundston and Riviere du Loup and who represent the bondholders living in London. These bonds are being purchased by the Canadian National. I would remind my colleagues of one other thing, and that is that the Canadian National Railways will receive value for every dollar spent in purchasing the Temiscouata railway. The equipment taken over is as follows: Five

locomotives to handle freight and two locomotives for passenger service; ten coaches; eighty freight cars; eleven miscellaneous units. In 1946 the railway handled 6,814 carloads of freight and 5,551 carloads of lumber or its by-products. In normal years upwards of 50,000 passengers were carried on the railway.
I repeat that it is far from being a losing proposition. If we look into the future we can see that it is bright because the necessary repairs and improvements will be made. They will not be so costly, after all. The member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) said one thing of which I took note, and that is that it is a public service to the people of the district. That is right. It is precisely for that reason that the Canadian National Railways have been so happy to agree to the suggestion made by the residents of the district, that the Temiscouata railway should be turned over to the Canadian National. The people of the district are grateful to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport and the government; they will be grateful to all hon. gentlemen who will support the measure and see that it is no longer delayed in passing all its stages.

I did, however, draw attention to the implications of federal government support. Since the matter was debated here last, however, I obtained from the office of the finance minister of British Columbia some information on the financial condition of the Pacific Great Eastern. A great deal of money has been put into it since 1916 when it was started. Its obligations accruing from loans for building and accrued interest since that time amount to over $115 million. Despite the increased revenue that may accrue to the road because of the extension, I am inclined to believe that deficits will continue to increase. As a matter of fact, I saw a communication in one of the British Columbia papers the other day that supported that view. I merely want to put myself on record here as not being opposed to this subsidy. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PROVISIONS TO SUBSIDIARY CORPORATIONS
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 174, to amend the Pension Fund Societies Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PROVISIONS TO SUBSIDIARY CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Is the minister not going to explain this bill?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PROVISIONS TO SUBSIDIARY CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
It is a very simple bill. It proposes merely to extend the benefits of the Pension Fund Societies Act to the employees of companies subsidiary to existing or perhaps future companies created by act of parliament, whether by special act or under the Companies Act.
This act has been on the statute books of Canada for some sixty years, and presently appears in the Revised Statutes of 1927 as chapter 155. The act provides that two or more of the senior employees of a Canadian corporation may form themselves into a pension fund society by the methods therein set

Pension Fund Societies Act forth, and the object of such a society is to create and administer a fund for the purpose of providing pensions for employees of the corporation who have become disabled through disability or age, and after their death to provide annuities for their widows and infant children and certain other relatives. The present act applies, but of course can only cover employees of the corporation itself. With the trend in modern business and the expansion of the ramifications of many of our corporations, in many cases covering a number of subsidiaries the control of the voting stock of which is held by what we might term the parent company, unfortunately under the existing law the employees of the subsidiary company cannot claim any benefits under the society that has been created by the parent company.
In order to enjoy the privileges which they may have under this Pension Fund Societies Act, it is necessary to pass an amendment to the act to bring them within the society that is already in existence under the authority of the parent company. I have in mind one company which has about six subsidiaries and, I understand, is desirous of taking advantage of this act for the benefit of its employees. If that company has to proceed under the existing law, it must create seven societies with seven boards of directors; seven annual meetings; seven sets of books and seven overhead expense accounts. The object of this section is merely to bring the employees of these subsidiaries within the provisions of the act for the purpose of giving them the benefits of the one society.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PROVISIONS TO SUBSIDIARY CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
I have not had an opportunity of reading this as carefully as I would have liked in conjunction with the original act. I noticed that the minister said this would apply to companies incorporated under a special act or under the Canadian Companies Act. Under the original act, which is chapter 155 of the Revised Statutes of 1927, perhaps I have not read it carefully enough, but I failed to find those words which the minister used. In other words, I do not find anything to indicate that they are the companies that are covered. Will the minister just direct me to that, because I think it is important to know it.
The second point upon which I wish to touch is that the addition to section 17 of chapter 155 which is provided for in the bill before us introduces certain rights and privileges to officers of the corporations affected. Again it may be that I have not read this chapter 155 carefully enough, but I do not find in it any similar provision in favour of the original beneficiaries under the

act. In other words, the members of the parent company should have those privileges set out here for the officers of the subsidiaries-that is correct?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PROVISIONS TO SUBSIDIARY CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PROVISIONS TO SUBSIDIARY CORPORATIONS
speechtext: What I want to be clear upon is this. Is there a similar provision in chapter 155 for those in the parent company, or are we introducing here a change in chapter 155 and merely making it apply to the subsidiaries? I confess to the minister that I have not read this act contained in chapter 155 as carefully as I should like, but I think the point should be answered.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PROVISIONS TO SUBSIDIARY CORPORATIONS
speechtext: I have not the act at hand, but my understanding is that the parent company will set up a pension fund society for that corporation. There are some twelve or thirteen of them in existence now. Then, in cases where that company or corporation has subsidiary companies, the employees of the subsidiary will have exactly the same rights in the existing pension fund society as those employed directly by the parent company.

The national library advisory committee, which the government appointed about a year ago, met in March last, and recommended that a bibliographic centre be established without delay. An appropriation of $18,950, included in the supplementary estimates submitted recently to the house, will enable a start to be made

I should like to make a statement to the government through the Secretary of State. I think that we are deficient in the matter of education in this country as compared with a great many other countries. When we talk about inequality of opportunity in the matter of education, I think we should talk about inequality in regard to the position of reading matter in the various provinces throughout Canada. If one looks at the statistics, one will find that the libraries in some provinces are stocked very differently, in proportion to population, than they are in others. I am only speaking from memory but in the province of Ontario, for instance, I think there is one book in the public library for each person of the population. That is not at all true in some of the other provinces.
I would suggest that when we are thinking about a national library and national culture some federal aid in the way of libraries would be about as good a thing as this government could do. By that I mean grants to libraries in some of what are called "have-not" provinces, so that the reading opportunities of people, and particularly young people in those provinces, could be equated more nearly to those provinces which can afford a greater supply of books. The building up of large libraries is important, but so is the proper selection, co-operation and expert help which will be available to those outlying libraries from a national institution such as a national library which we envisage here at Ottawa. While I admit

Supply-Secretary of State that a research library in the capital of this country is a tremendously important thing, I am not prepared to grant that it is the most important work that a national library can do. I think the most important work a national library can do is to aid and to help libraries in those outlying parts so that the great bulk of our population, which after all is not settled in Ottawa, may have the use of these facilities.
