The house resumed from Friday, November 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. May-bank for the second reading of Bill No. 66, respecting Alberta Natural Gas Company.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak in this debate because prior to coming to this house my work had been principally with labour and industry and I hoped that my major address this session would be concerning such matters. However on Tuesday evening the hon. member for Vancouver East said certain things which I felt reflected, not oniy on the integrity of the British Columbia members but on our desire to serve our province and serve it well.
I am sure the people of my riding have considerable interest in this pipe line matter and they would be happy to see a pipe line built through the Crowsnest pass. I am sure even the coal miners who are producing a competitive fuel, but who are so notoriously progressive in their thinking, would be happy to have such a convenient fuel as gas available for their furnaces and kitchens. I know the people farther west in my riding at Kimberley, Cranbrook and the other smaller towns would be happy to have such a convenient fuel at their disposal.
Previous to rising to speak tonight I undertook considerable research in order to determine if what I considered were the facts were true. I feel that what I am going to say will be as close to the facts as anything I have heard in this chamber during this debate.
On Monday, March 21, 1949, the Pipe Lines Act was given first reading in this house and it subsequently was passed. The purpose of that legislation was to provide for the control of international and interprovincial trade through pipe lines. In order to set up a company under that act it is necessary that a bill pass this house. In other words, the company must be chartered.
Before being permitted to do business the company must prove, first, that they have a definite supply of gas or oil available; that they have obtained the consent of the government of Alberta or any other province to take such gas or oil out of the province; that they have obtained a permit from the Department of Trade and Commerce in connection with the gas or oil which they wish to take out of Canada; that they are properly financed for such an undertaking; and that they have available markets.
In March of the same year a bill was before this house to incorporate the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited. I have gone through that bill thoroughly and nowhere can I find that a route has been designated. That bill resembles almost word for word the bill now before the house to incorporate Alberta Natural Gas Company. I repeat that in neither of those bills is a route definitely
Alberta Natural Gas Company designated. Therefore I think it could be safely said that Westcoast Transmission Company Limited could build a pipe line through any territory and in any direction it might choose, provided it obtained the permission of the board of transport commissioners.
As I said, I have conducted some research. In the files of the transport board I found an application which had been made to the board by the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited on May 11, 1949, a copy of which I have on my desk. That application was to transport gas from Edmonton in the province of Alberta to a point in the vicinity of Kings-gate in the province of British Columbia, with a branch line from a point in the vicinity of Kingsgate to cover Trail in British Columbia. I know Kingsgate quite well. It is a beautiful little town which is a port of entry to the United States, but I am sure the population is not large enough to warrant its being a terminal of a gas pipe line.
I know they have not pressed their application for permission to build this pipe line, but I am sure their inactivity in that regard is not merely coincidental with the arguments that are being presented at the present time by those who oppose this bill. The only objection I have heard to the passage of the bill before us is that this company will export gas to the United States if they obtain permission from the transport board. As I have said, the two bills are as much alike as two peas. I could go farther than that and say that they are as much alike as two divorce bills such as those that pass this house so rapidly, although we have had difficulty with them on occasion. But there is one outstanding difference. The bill to incorporate the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited has passed the house whereas the bill to incorporate Alberta Natural Gas Company has not. Now if we have no faith in the board of transport commissioners, our natural heritage is already lost, and to pass another bill to charter another company could have little effect in this regard.

Is the hon. member aware that the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited to which he refers made application to the transport board in September to build a pipe line following an entirely northern route through Canada?

I think that question will be answered by the remainder of my remarks. This present bill may be some indication that the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited cannot meet the requirements I have enumerated earlier. If that is so they would be precluded from obtaining a licence to transmit gas.

Alberta Natural Gas Company
It is significant that the Westcoast Transmission Company, which obtained its charter in March of this year, has yet to receive a permit. They requested that their original application for a permit to construct a pipe line through central British Columbia be withdrawn. Some members put forward the view that a line should be built through the province of British Columbia. It is a point of view with which I certainly wholeheartedly agree. They argued that we should supply Canadian industries first. They should not be so naive. It may be that it cannot be agreed by the companies and the board that such a line is practical, possibly in view of the fact that their markets must be in British Columbia and also in the northwest portion of the United States. If they should find it is impractical to transport gas by one particular route, then an alternative certainly would be necessary. If it were made absolutely statutory that a pipe line to supply such markets must be built in any one particular direction, then if it could not be built at competitive prices there would be no pipe line at all. I say that as long as we are sure the needs of Canada will be served first, regardless of the route, then there must be some alternative.
There is an age-old argument that the railways were built to develop the country regardless of cost. I do not feel that holds true in this case. We must remember that prior to the railways being built there was no other method of transportation unless we consider the covered wagon and the oxcart. I am quite sure hon. members will agree such transportation offered no competition whatsoever to the railways. It must be remembered there is a competitive field in British Columbia and the Pacific northwest. For example, there is the question of coal. I think if I were going to raise an objection to this or any other pipe line bill it would be on the basis that possibly it might deprive some of my constituents of a job, but I am sure they are sufficiently progressive that they would not ask me to take such a stand. We have coal, wood, sawdust, tremendous hydroelectric power, and in the foreseeable future atomic power. If a pipe line cannot be built at a cost sufficiently low to compete with such fuels, then a pipe line will not be built at all.
I was not a member of the house when a charter was granted to the Westcoast Transmission Company, but I understand the bill passed with little opposition. Therefore I had assumed that any other such bills would pass with little opposition, and that even a second or third charter could be granted. It is my considered opinion that anyone opposing the measure at this time is committing an offence against our system either wittingly

or unwittingly, and is helping to set up a Canadian monopoly in the pipe line business. We have been asked why we are silent on this matter. I think there was considerable reason to be silent. I felt any comments on this measure were absolutely unnecessary. As I said earlier, however, there were accusations in the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). In that speech he said, at page 2101 of Hansard:
Somebody is going to have to be paid for the money spent in presenting the petition to parliament. Somebody will have to be paid for the cost of all the lobbying that has been done around here during the past several weeks. I should like to know who is paying for those things and how they are going to recoup themselves if they do not ultimately build a pipe line.
I suppose that would be their business anyway.
That is something the sponsors of these bills should tell us. That is something the British Columbia members who have so little regard for the welfare of British Columbia that they vote for these bills should tell us. They should make it quite clear to the house just whom they are supporting in this matter, British Columbia or some pipe line promoters.
I consider that a fairly serious charge, and I wish those who hear me now to consider seriously what I am going to say. I think, in the light of all the related facts,
I may ask with equal justification whether those British Columbia members who are opposing the granting of these charters are doing so for the welfare of British Columbia; or are they supporting some British Columbia pipe line promoters? One hon. member from the Liberal benches rose to point out he was wholeheartedly in agreement with the opposition on this question. I am very happy there are not more Liberals taking that position because I would say that it is an obviously biased and reactionary position, and if there were more I would be extremely apprehensive of the future of the Liberal party.

Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of filibustering this bill. I have some pretty strong opinions on the matter now before the house. I want to assure the house, and particularly the member who has just taken his seat, that I have no personal interest whatsoever in the bill, but I am concerned about the principles that these bills are establishing. These pipe lines will not in any way affect the part of the country I represent, but we have seen the development of the resources of that part of the country manipulated over the years in exactly the same way that these bills attempt to manipulate the resources of Alberta.
The hon. member who has just xaken his seat is new here. I guess he is completely

honest in what he has said, but I can assure him he has a lot to learn about finagling on the part of high finance.
And the government.
He is honest but he is green.

If I could make myself believe the statement he has just made was correct I would be quite willing to sit down. The act to which he has referred that was passed in April merely gave the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada the right to issue licences to companies such as those mentioned in these bills. If those who desire to establish pipe lines could now go to the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada and have the provisions of this bill implemented by the board, then these measures would not be before the house.
The hon. member also said that the five bills which came in the back door from the Senate at the last session of parliament passed the house with little opposition. There was not much chance to offer any opposition.
You voted for them.

No, I did not. You will find that on April 29, 1949, I am recorded in Hansard as having made some fairly strong statements against them. They came in the back door on April 28 and this house prorogued on April 30. There was little discussion on them in the house. At that time we moved an amendment against them. They were sent to a standing committee, were considered there overnight, and were passed by the house the next morning. My opposition to them at that time was based on the fact that there were members of parliament then in the house who would not be members any longer after a day or two, and had no right to bind the people of Canada or the House of Commons to this type of legislation. Many of them would not be coming back; yet we were saddling the present House of Commons with legislation which I figured, on more mature judgment and with more time at our disposal in which to analyse the manoeuvring behind those bills, would not have passed. They received very little discussion or consideration, but were opposed by this group as strongly as we could oppose them in the time at our disposal; and we moved amendments to them.
The bill now before the house is exactly the same as the one we discussed Tuesday evening, and exactly the same as the four we discussed in April, 1949. I want to stress the point as far as this bill is concerned, and the other four I mentioned, that they are merely stock promotion bills. There is no capital behind them. My hon. friend said
Alberta Natural Gas Company that in effect, while opposing bills of this type, we were building up a monopoly in Canada, but in my opinion the reverse is true. It seems to me that the company incorporated under Bill No. 238, the only one with capital behind it, will finish up with the one pipe line in this country. We are asked to pass these other bills incorporating companies with no capital behind them, and giving them the right to go out and sell shares. The people who have the $4,500,000 with which to gamble, the people who were incorporated under Bill No. 238, will buy the stock of these companies and in the final analysis all the stock will be owned, controlled or held by one company. That is what we want to avoid.
I think the history of this country should show us very clearly that the time has come when governments, both provincial and federal, should have some regard to our natural resources. It is all right to talk about free enterprise and smaller organizations operating under charter, but when you are juggling with the natural resources belonging to the people they have a right to expect their elected representatives to see that those resources are protected and developed in their interests, with some control by the legislative bodies of the country to see that they are used as they should be.
As an example I should like to refer briefly to the coal mines of Nova Scotia. When the leases were first given out-in that case there were leases rather than bills -there were half a dozen or a dozen operating coal companies in the maritime provinces. There was competition. They sent out sales agents; they sold coke; operations were carried on as we are led to believe would be the case in connection with the oil resources of Alberta if these bills should pass. But after a few years one major company, Dominion Coal, began to buy the stock of the smaller companies. When they had a sufficient amount of stock the smaller shareholders were squeezed out. They lost their investment, and the industry wound up with one over-all operating corporation. This type of legislation is exactly the same in principle, except that here we are doing it on a national scale.
As far as I am concerned, if I could imagine for a moment that there would be six or seven operating companies with pipe lines in Canada I should say that would be a good development, that would be decentralized control of that resource. But I cannot see it operating in that way. I am as sure as I am that I am standing here that before many years go by there will be one pipe line in this country, owned and controlled by

Alberta Natural Gas Company Standard Oil of the United States through Imperial Oil, its Canadian subsidiary. By these bills we are simply legalizing the right of these stock promoters to go out and sell stock, because there is no capital behind them, no money involved at all. The oil companies are the people who have the money. They will buy this stock; there will be one operating pipe line in the country, and that is about all you will ever get out of this sort of development.
My purpose in rising at this time, Mr. Speaker, was to move an amendment. I stress, as we always have stressed in this house, the desirability of public ownership or some public control when this type of legislation is proposed. That is based on long experience with this kind of legislation, knowing the damage it can do and the difficulty of getting rid of it once it is established. When I move my amendment hon. members may vote for it or not, as they like; but if this development goes ahead in spite of the opposition we are able to offer, in the years to come I think the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) will look back at Hansard and say, "Well, I was young and a bit naive at that time, but I can put it down to inexperience; and those fellows were right." I thought I saw signs of the fine hand of the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) in some of the phrasing we heard not long ago. He did not do a bad job, either. In the years to come, if I am not here-it will be because age has defeated me-my hon. friend will be able to read Hansard and I am sure he will say, "Why, my advisers at that time were not so farsighted. The people who opposed that legislation and attempted to amend it had pretty good judgment. I am sorry I did not listen to them." So I move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce):
That this bill be not now read a second time but that further consideration thereof be deferred until this house has had an opportunity to record its opinion that consideration should be given to the construction and operation of pipe lines by a crown corporation, or to a public agency owned and controlled by the government of Canada.
To anticipate hon. members who may go to Beauchesne and Bourinot and May and then back to Walpole, I want to say that an amendment similar to this was moved last session by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, Mr. Young.

Studying law, so he may come back here and understand Beauchesne. On

April 29, 1949, he moved a similar amendment, which appears at page 2775 of Hansard, reading as follows:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the construction and operation of pipe lines by a crown corporation or other public agency owned and controlled by the government of Canada.
That amendment was held to be in order, and was voted upon. I have even softened my amendment a little. That amendment asked that the bill be not now read a second time. I believe that action on this particular bill should be deferred until the house has had an opportunity of recording its opinion. These bills should be sent to a committee. We have lots of time; there is no hurry about this. I am sure every member of this house wants to do the proper thing with these bills. The bill we discussed on Tuesday night, and the one we are discussing now, should be handed to a committee so that the members can meet the people who are sponsoring this legislation. These measures could then be returned to the house with sufficient information to assure the members that they are either good or bad. If the facts are given to the average member, I believe he is reasonable enough to form an opinion that is in the best interests of the people of this country. This amendment merely suggests that we defer action to permit a committee to consider the bill. Later on, we can record an opinion based on the evidence given to us by the people who are capable of doing it, and who have the facts. So far that has not been done.
The question is on the amendment moved by Mr. Gillis. All those in favour will please say yea.
Yea.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this measure this evening. I listened with a good deal of interest to the remarks of the member of Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne). He is a new member in this house and I think he meant what he said, but there were some inaccuracies in his statements which will appear as I explain the different facts in connection with this measure.

I believe, as conscientiously as it is possible for one to believe, that this bill should not be passed at this session. I believe that the questions raised by this bill are of the utmost importance, perhaps as important as any questions that will be considered by this house during the whole life of this parliament. This evening I shall try to point out some of those considerations which I believe are of such great importance.
In the first place, it is quite clear that any pipe line which would be laid by the Alberta Natural Gas Company will go to the boundary between Canada and the United States at the first convenient point. From there it will be continued into the United States. There is a possibility that a branch of the main pipe line will be laid back to the Canadian cities on the Pacific coast. There is also a possibility, although I think it is very remote, that a branch line may also be laid up the valley of the Columbia into the district around Trail.
Surely there can be no question that the objective of this company is to get a natural gas and oil pipe line into the northwestern states of the United States of America; that has never been denied. Many hints have been made to the contrary but, in my opinion, there is not the slightest doubt that the purpose of this company is to lay a pipe line to supply the northwestern states of the United States. I know that because about two years ago there were lobbyists in Ottawa, and they came to see me as a British Columbia member. I queried them as to whether this pipe line was to serve Canada or the United States, and they said, "Oh, well, it is to go to the United States but eventually it will get up to Vancouver." That was the plan of the promoters of this company a year and a half or two years ago.
It was interesting to listen to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) describe just where this pipe line was to go. At page 2109 of Hansard he pointed out that there was a natural route for a pipe line through the Yellowhead pass, down through the centre of British Columbia and eventually to the coast cities. I believe that is the route which should be followed by a pipe line. Then he went on to say that there was another route which would start in southern Alberta, and he defined the start of the route clearly. It would start at Pincher Creek, Alberta, and go through the Crowsnest pass to Frank, then into Cranbrook and Kimberley.
At that point the minister began to get quite hazy. He stopped dealing with geographical locations and began to give hazy directions-the sort of directions which if
Alberta Natural Gas Company one took to find a place would certainly land him at some other place. It reminded me of being given the wrong directions in the army. He said it would go from Kimberley down the west side of the interior. What he meant by the "west side of the interior" is anyone's guess. At page 2110 of Hansard he said:
Anyone who knows anything about British Columbia knows that it is a province of mountains and valleys. It would be utterly impossible to put a pipe line through in just one direction. In my opinion the proper way is to go south and then north into the Kootenay and Okanagan valleys, to go from the south to the north.
The minister was going north and south, and then south and north, but the one thing he neglected to say was that the route would go south into the United States, and then there might be a branch line north into British Columbia. His description was so confusing that even the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), who is rather quick at understanding these things, was misled into thinking the minister said the route would go through British Columbia. Actually, the second route mentioned by the Minister of Fisheries is obviously a route through the United States.
I should like to say a word about who is behind this proposed company. I have in my hand a dispatch from the Financial Times of November 25, 1949. It is headed "Natural Gas lines form major group of public utilities". It points out that natural gas lines are now becoming of the utmost importance on this continent, and that they are going to be among the very biggest groups of business. This is not small business we are dealing with at all when we are dealing with these pipe lines. It is business which is going to involve hundreds of millions of dollars and the jobs of hundreds of thousands of Canadians. We are not just dealing with some little side show. This article points out that there is a Westcoast Transmission Company which was granted a charter last spring, and goes on to say:
Westcoast Transmission Company proposes to export gas to British Columbia and United States areas in the northwest . . . The company's plans, which have been approved by the dominion parliament, call for an all-Canadian route, from north central Alberta through British Columbia and1 include numerous retail facilities along the way . . . Total mileage 1,100 miles and total estimated cost $170 million.
Then it goes on to describe the other pipe line, the one which we are discussing tonight:
The Northwest Natural Gas Company, an American concern, expects to export gas via Kingsgate, B.C.-
Which is in the riding of Kootenay East.
-to the state of Washington. Chances for this company do not appear so good, since its plans call for export of Alberta gas primarily to the United

Alberta Natural Gas Company
States, without giving consideration, to the same extent as other companies in the field, to the real needs of Canadian provinces. Total cost $100 million.
It also deals with Prairie Pipe Lines Limited, the other company which is seeking a charter, and says:
The Prairie Pipe Lines Limited, whose plans have not yet found the full approval of the parliament at the time of writing, also call for export of natural gas to Washington state and for re-import of part of this gas to southern B.C.
The Northwest Natural Gas Company which, I suggest, is behind Alberta Natural Gas Company-if it is not, let the members who are sponsoring this bill get up and say who is behind the Alberta Natural Gas Company-is a subsidiary of Venezuela Syndicate Incorporated of New York. If hon. members care to look up Moody's Manual of Investments, 1949, they will find, at page 857, the particulars of Venezuela Syndicate Incorporated. We are dealing here in effect with a United States corporation. The natural gas is not to go through United States in bond to another point in Canada, which is the way the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said that the oil was to go from Gretna, Manitoba, to Superior, Wisconsin, and so to Sarnia. That is not the case here. I do not believe it is the case with the oil pipe line either. I think the bulk of that oil is going to the Chicago area. But this gas is not to go in bond through the United States from one Canadian point to another. It is to go to the northwestern United States to develop the states of Washington and Oregon which are in direct competition with the province of British Columbia in practically every line of our endeavour.
Then there is another consideration. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, with that promptness and readiness with which he so often gives assurances which never turn out to be of much value, assured us one evening that he would see to it that Vancouver got this gas before any went to the United States; that Vancouver would be looked after in any event. That of course was an absurd statement. All that the Minister of Trade and Commerce can do is to give or to withhold a permit for the export of gas. Once he has given that permit for the export of gas, he has no way of forcing it back into Canada. That brings me to this further question. If Canada is to have gas and oil lines across
[Mr. Green.1

States government or of the Canadian government. It is in the hands of these oil and gas companies. They are setting policy at the present time and the fact that there is no international agreement alone justifies a delay in dealing with these bills.

That is not the responsibility of the province of Alberta. It is the responsibility of the Canadian parliament under the system which is being followed. The only sort of measures that the province of Alberta can enact, or any other provincial government, are based on the conservation of natural gas. They might bring in a regulation and say: We will impose this restriction in order to conserve natural gas. But when they go further and use that power to stop the movement of natural gas into another province or into the United States they are exceeding their power. That is not within their jurisdiction. I submit that they cannot control the export of these commodities, and therefore the responsibility rests here with the Canadian parliament.

I shall not take much of the time of the committee. Since we are hearing so much being said about Canadian citizenship and about the building of a proposed national gallery, I submit, sir, that one of the most important matters is the study of the history of this country. I knew intimately the first archivist, Sir Arthur Doughty, who succeeded in making so many important historical documents available to the Canadian people. I wonder how many of my colleagues knew Sir Arthur Doughty personally. He and Adam Shortt working together published real treasures of history from the beginning of the country. Anybody knows how difficult it is for anyone to study in the parliamentary library, which is one of the richest in this country, or to go to the expense of going to the archives to take notes there of all the documents on the past history of this country. Doughty and Shortt succeeded in having most important documents published under the title of "Constitutional Papers" or "Constitutional Documents". A few of the documents were published each year in the annual report of the archives,

but we now find that some of the most historical documents are difficult to get. The publication of these documents was discontinued, either on account. of the war or for some other reason, and the result is that they are not now available to Canadian students. In my humble opinion this publication should be resumed from the point at which it was stopped, in order that all Canadians who want to know something about the history of their country may have easy access to them.
The new Secretary of State is doing very well at the head of his department and I congratulate him. I wish him every success, but I do hope he will give definite instruction that the publication of these historical documents be resumed at the earliest possible date from the time the previous publication was stopped. I make this suggestion in order to promote a greater knowledge of the history of this country by our young people from Newfoundland to British Columbia. Some of these publications are quite difficult to get and perhaps a reprinting may be necessary. Many young people who want to study these things cannot afford the heavy travelling expense of coming to Ottawa. These documents should be available in the home, in the college or wherever it may be necessary in order to promote knowledge of the history of Canada.
Could the Secretary of State tell us how many people have been working at the archives cataloguing the correspondence of Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier? What amount was paid for their services? How many people have been working during the last few years cataloguing the correspondence of Mr. King? At the present time historical documents are made available only after fifty years and in my humble opinion they should be available to the people almost immediately. We now have access to the correspondence of Sir John A. Macdonald who died more than fifty years ago and to part of the correspondence of Sir Wilfrid Laurier who died exactly thirty years ago. Sir Wilfrid lived a long time and some of his correspondence, particularly about the Manitoba school question and other matters, should be made available to the public.

As I said this afternoon, the papers of both Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier are in order. As yet there is not a complete catalogue prepared, but any of the papers that are available can be seen by anyone who wishes to see them. All of Sir John's documents are available, but not Sir Wilfrid Laurier's, because some of them are not yet fifty years old.

I think it would be impossible to say just what it has cost to put these documents in order and prepare them for examination because the work was done under votes which included the activities of other public officials. The number of officials first employed in looking after Mr. King's papers was three. That was back in 1946, and the number has since been increased to four.
How much are they paid?
In 1946-47 they received $3,613; in 1947-48 the amount paid was $8,244; in 1948-49, $10,059; and in 1949-50 up to October 31, $6,680.

I thank the minister, but I think that is costing much more than the correspondence is worth. I suggest to him that he stop that expenditure now so that any expenditure necessary will be borne by those who will be reading the correspondence. We are being asked to spend money each year in preparing that correspondence but we cannot see it.

speechtext: I should like to say a few words with respect to item 50. As I understand, there is in the civil service what is known as a quota system. I believe the effect of the quota system is that in the various departments of the government, not just in the office of the civil service commission itself but in all departments, only a certain percentage of the employees can be permanent. The remainder have to be listed as temporary employees. The result is that many people are temporary for years and years. They are permanent in many respects but not legally, and not so far as pension rights are concerned. I should like to know what progress has been made in recent years by way of increasing the percentage of employees who can be classified as permanent. For example, what was the percentage of permanent employees to the entire civil service two years ago? What was the percentage a year ago, and what is it now?

May I give some information on this subject? The number of temporaries in each department can be explained in different ways. The establishment of each department is not only decided upon by the civil service commission after it investigates the needs of the department for permanent and temporary positions, but their report is submitted to the treasury board. The treasury board officials then inquire into the requirements of this department, and decide on the establishment as a whole, as between permanents and temporaries.
Before the war those departments would have their establishments on a percentage quota; some would have seventy per cent permanents and thirty per cent temporaries, and so on. When the war came along, to protect

the rights and privileges of those who were in the armed forces, the civil commission made no permanent appointments-perhaps the occasional one, but very few. At that time thousands of temporary employees were hired. After the war the commission and the government of the day applied the veterans' preference, and those men were brought in but could not become permanent without having at least one year of service. The temporaries employed during the war were replaced by veterans, and as the need for permanents developed in the departments those veterans became permanent.
I do not suppose there are two departments in which the percentages as between permanent and temporary employees are the same. I do not think the civil service commission should take the blame for the number of permanents or temporaries in the department because, in the final analysis, they do not make the decision. It is the treasury board that decides.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The quota may differ as between different branches of the same department.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister has told us that these quotas vary from branch to branch and department to department, but some of that information should be available to us. Among civil servants this is a rather sore point. After all, as members of parliament, surely it is within our province to be concerned about the morale of civil servants, and this quota system is one of the things that affect morale.

There is always a good defence for every action of the government. My hon. friends of the C.C.F. who, if they could, would have a socialist state in this country, would proceed along the line that everyone who works for the government should be on a permanent basis. The hon. member has asked something about the quota system and I will give him an example by referring to the Department of National Revenue.
The quota of permanents for that department is quite low at the moment, approximately 40 per cent. There is a reason for that. On the taxation side there were as many as 11,600 employees in the department because of the backlog of business that had accumulated during the war years. That backlog of business will be accomplished by the end of this fiscal year and we can carry on exactly the same duties that we are doing now with probably two-thirds of that number or at least with about 75 per cent. I ask hon. members this question, as a matter of good business. Would it have been good business to have all of these employees permanent when we knew absolutely that within two or three years we would carry on the business of that department with 8,000 people instead of 12,000 people? From the point of view of economy and of saving the taxpayers' money, it would have been sheer folly to give those people the idea that at some time or other they would be permanent officials. On the other hand, it is the only means whereby there can be some latitude in weeding out.

Supply-Civil Service Commission All people who work for the government are not of the highest calibre, although in general they are. People who are in private business or in industry have a perfect right to dismiss employees if they are not giving competent service. But once somebody gets into a government department, is in a permanent position, and has become a permanent employee, you are hamstrung and you are tied right there if you try to promote efficiency in the department, because he is in there feeling that he has a comfortable seat for the rest of his life.
Does the minister mean that his permanent employees are inefficient?
No.
No, I do not. I think that all of my permanent employees are highly efficient.
Why should that not happen with the others?

But there would be no use in giving those who are not permanent employees the inducement that because they had gotten into the department, they could become permanent employees just because they were there. There is not the need for them. As between one department of government and another, if some people are supernumerary, they are transferred. We make a request to the civil service commission to transfer them to another department where there will be work for them. The point I want to make is that from the point of view both of economy and of efficiency it is not in the best interest of the government to have 100 per cent permanency in any department.
Will the minister tell me if they have any difficulty in getting applicants for those various jobs in his department?
No, not the slightest difficulty.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I realize that perhaps it is unfair for us to ask the Secretary of State about this matter on this particular discussion; but I think it is a matter that has not been discussed enough in the House of Commons, at least during the period that I have been here.

During the war period it was necessary to extend the departments of government, to organize new ones and to take pretty much what you could get. But I think the time has arrived when this matter of civil servants, how they are employed and what their terms of employment are is one for the House of Commons to give serious consideration to.
I know that the methods of employing civil servants through the civil service commission outside the House of Commons and in a large part of the country leave much to be desired, and that the commission is not considered to be the impartial body that it is supposed to be. The Minister of Public Works, who is not here at the present time, undertook to answer for the Secretary of State; and in my opinion he made a worse job of it than would have been made if he had left the Secretary of State alone. The Secretary of State was not doing so badly. He at least was careful in his answers. But his adviser, when he took over, laid great stress on the fact that the civil service commission did the employing, that the civil service commission set the quotas, and that the civil service commission was all-supreme. Then in the next breath he said that the civil service commission had nothing to do with it, that treasury board is supreme, and that in the final analysis "we five men make the decision".
An. hon. Member: Six.

Five and himself. The civil service commission, I believe, employs approximately 122,000 people. Of those, 40,000 have been employed in some capacity in the government service under the commission for the last ten years. They go back in their employment previous to the war. So the Minister of Public Works cannot write that situation off by saying that, with the veterans coming back, preference had to be retained for them. That 40,000 were employed previous to the war, and they are still temporaries. They cannot become permanent until the treasury board says so. The chiefs of the departments who work with the personnel who are taken in under the terms of the commission know the qualifications of these employees. Why should the final say in determining whether they are essential and should be permanent or not rest with six men who have nothing to do with most of them? That is something which should be corrected. The Minister of Public Works made it quite clear that not for reasons of efficiency but for reasons of economy they say they are not needed, whether departments are crippled or otherwise.
Supply-Civil Service Commission
While the Secretary of State indicates that there are some 40,000 temporaries, many instances will be found of people who are only six months, and sometimes less than that, employees of the department under the civil service commission and who are made permanent at very good salaries, while those who are performing essential services drag along for over ten years and never become permanent.
I agree with the Minister of National Revenue that, no matter whether they are designated as permanent or not, if they are not fulfilling the duties of the position that they occupy and there is reason to dismiss them, the fact that they are permanent employees should not interfere with it. I have no hesitation in saying that nobody should be put on a job and be told that he is going to stay there permanently, and because he is a permanent employee he can sit around and do nothing. I do not think it is fair to anyone who has supervision over a department. A certain amount of work has to be performed. The probationary period of an employee should not be longer than a year. The chief of a department and the head of the civil service commission should know in a year whether an employee is good, bad or indifferent. If he measures up and performs his duties he should be made permanent after a year's employment. They should not go along for a longer period than that. The fact that an employee is permanent should not preclude his dismissal if there is cause for it.
The permanent employee who has more security is a much better employee than a person who is sitting around for ten years in an insecure position, not knowing where he fits in. That employee is not much good. I am just a human being, and if I were in that position I would be watching for a better position than the one that I occupied. I would be looking for the time when I would have to get out. There is something wrong with a job or with a person who drags along for ten years and is not entitled to the rights and privileges that are given to other employees in the organization.
We have to do a lot more talking about this kind of thing. Government in Canada is becoming quite a large organization. I have always looked on this House of Commons as a trades union of the civil servants who are employed under the regulations laid down by this house. We are the people who should be protecting them. We make these laws. We should not leave it to any six-man board to have the final say on the future of thousands of people who are rendering essential service in this country; and we should not be keeping

Supply-Civil Service Commission them in the insecure position in which they are today, without the provisions of the superannuation allowance. That is all I have to say on the subject tonight. In the future we are going to have a lot more to say about it. I just wanted to say this because I think the Minister of Public Works did not do as good a job as he thought he did. I am sorry he left the chamber.

There is another matter in connection with superannuation in the civil service that I wish to say a few words about. The superannuation act was amended in 1947 in order to make provision for the superannuation of veterans. A return which I received a short time ago indicates that very few veterans are taking advantage of the Civil Service Superannuation Act. I asked the department how many active service veterans of world war I, who were not in the civil service prior to enlistment, but who had subsequently joined the civil service, applied for superannuation benefits under the superannuation act. This is the information I received. In the Department of Agriculture there were 423 veterans who joined that department after returning from overseas. Of that number only 53 have taken advantage of the superannuation act. I will not give all the departments. In the comptroller of the treasury branch there were 231 in that category. Seventy-three applied to take advantage of the act. In the fisheries department there were 70 and only seven are taking advantage of the superannuation act. In the penitentiaries commission there were 257
2270	HOUSE OF
Supply-Civil Service Commission returned men and only 43 are taking advantage of the act. I could go all through the different departments. They all indicate about the same percentage. This must surely indicate to the minister that the section of the act which was passed for the benefit of veterans is not really doing for them what it was intended to do.
Is there any intention to amend this act so that it will benefit the veterans, as I am sure the intention was. The chief reason why these men are not taking advantage of the act is that it is costing them far more for their annuity than they should pay. For instance, the act provides that during the time they were overseas they contribute not only their own assessment but the assessment which the government would have to pay. Besides that they have to pay four per cent interest on all that contribution over a long period of years. Many of these men did not join the government service for five, ten or fifteen years after they left the service and the result in many cases is that they are paying $1,000 or more above what they should have to pay to provide for the annuity which the act is supposed to give them. I should like to ask the Secretary of State if this matter has been called to his attention and if it is intended to make proper provision for these cases.
The matter has not been called to my attention. This concerns the superannuation act and would be a matter for the Department of Finance.

Has the head of a department the right to make a temporary employee a permanent employee? The other day I had occasion to go to a department where there were three or four temporary employees who had been employed for four or five years and who were anxious to become permanent. The head of the department told me that it was


his prerogative to make those people permanent. I asked him how that would be done and he told me it would be by recommendation to the civil service commission. He told me that it would then go to the treasury board. That is taking the right away from a commission and giving it to government patronage.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Nonsense.

If the treasury board makes the final ruling, then that ruling is being made by politicians at the top and not by the commission. If it is made by the head of the department, nine times out of ten he is a political appointee and he would make his recommendation on that basis.
The head of the department may make a recommendation and then the civil service decides on the appointment provided that it is within the quota set by the treasury board.

I am glad the king's printer is in front of the Secretary of State in case he is needed to answer some questions I should like to ask. I understand it has been a practice at the printing bureau, for as long a time as some people can remember, to pay overtime at the rate of time and a half for the first three hours after the regular quitting time and double time after that. If an employee of the printing bureau is called in earlier than the usual time at which he goes to work, that is paid for at double time. The statement I have made as to payment of time and a half for the first three hours after the regular quitting time and double time after that is substantiated by sessional paper 106C which was tabled on April 4, 1949.
My information is that some changes have been made in connection with this matter, or shall I be extremely cautious and say that at the present time there is great uncertainty about the payment for overtime to employees at the printing bureau. It appears that there are a couple of orders in council which may have some bearing on the matter. One is order in council P.C. 1/4646 of September 13, 1949, and the other is order in council P.C. 4840 of September 20, 1949. The first of these orders in council relates to employees at the printing bureau while the second is of general application to prevailing rates employees.
It seems that as a result of these two orders in council certain changes have been made at the printing bureau with regard to overtime rates of pay. As I say, the long-established practice is that the overtime rate began, to

quote the language of sessional paper 106C of April 4, 1949, "after the regular quitting time". Whenever that regular quitting time was over, if employees were asked to work another hour or two or three they were to be paid at overtime rates. Apparently as a result of these orders in council it is now the case that, if a man for any reason is not there to start work at the regular time of commencement, he has to work that night or after the regular quitting time, the amount of time that he was late before the overtime rates begin. May I say at the moment I am not arguing the pros or cons of the case. I do not think I need to. I am simply pointing out that a change has been made, and it was made without consulting the employees concerned.
Another point that has been drawn to my attention is that there has also been a change with respect to the rate of pay when employees are called in ahead of time. I understand it has been the custom through the years that, if it were necessary to ask a printer at the bureau to come in ahead of time, perchance because Hansard gets thicker with these all-day sessions, he was to be paid double time for that previous time. I am told they are now being called in ahead of time and are being asked to work any previous hours for straight time.
I have made these remarks in the form of statements. I could have put them in question form, but these are the points that have been drawn to my, attention. I believe they are correct. At least there is uncertainty about them, right at this very time. If I am wrong the Secretary of State can get the information from the king's printer and correct me. If I am right it seems to me that the matter should be given consideration. It is not conducive to the best morale amongst working forces to change long established conditions and customs, particularly when they relate to the rate of pay.
Another point concerning which there is dissatisfaction amongst the employees at the printing bureau has to do with the differential between the day rate and the night rate. Some hon. members may recall that I put quite a lengthy table on Hansard last spring having to do with this matter and pointing to the discrepancies between the rates of pay at _ the government printing bureau and at printing offices in Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal. I may say the reason I name these cities is because the Public Printing and Stationery Act names Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal as a standard for rates at the printing bureau.
As I pointed out when I put these figures on Hansard before, employees at the printing buieau get a little less than is the case in
Supply-Civil Service Commission each of these three cities. From time to time under the general practice having to do with prevailing rates employees, the rates have been increased, but there has always been a time lag. Last April, however, a welcome increase came through, but since then there has been a change made in the differential between day and night employees. I believe the previous plan was in existence for a long time. Evidence of the old plan was given in the sessional paper to which I have referred and which was tabled on April 4, 1949. It said that the rate for night work was 25 per cent over the day rate. As I say, that 25 per cent differential ^ has obtained for a good many years. Just recently it has been reduced to 15 per cent. One of the reasons which has been indicated to the employees at the printing bureau for the reduction from 25 per cent to 15 per cent is that 15 per cent is the differential in effect at the printing shop in the patent record office. The answer to that is that over the years it has been recognized, and I may say recognized by the printers in the patent record office as well, that the strain of the work at the printing bureau, particularly during the months when the House of Commons is in session, is such that night work well deserves the 25 per cent differential.
I have done it before, and so have other members, but I think that again we should pay tribute to the efficiency of the printing bureau. Some of the things I am saying may indicate that I am a little bit critical of the king's printer himself because he is the administrative head of the bureau, but I want to include him with all of the employees. I want to say that they do a mighty good job especially when we consider that after these all-day sessions of the house we have the complete Hansard delivered to us next morning together with all the other documents we require. I wish Hansard could record the applause being given my remarks because it means that my statement meets with the approval of members generally.
May I suggest that working at the printing bureau these nights is a pretty tough racket, and that the 25 per cent differential is more than deserved. I should like to hear some explanation as to why it was reduced to 15 per cent, and I hope that it can be restored.
There are one or two other things that are also of concern. I may have to come back to them later but I shall mention them now. One is the feeling on the part of the employees at the printing bureau that the forty hour week should be instituted without delay. I know that at times when printers have asked for a forty hour week, and other trade

Supply-Civil Service Commission union workers for that matter, employers have said:	All you want is to reduce the
number of hours you work regularly so that you can start drawing overtime sooner. Workers in a good many trades, and particularly in the printing trade, have demonstrated across the country that when they ask for a forty hour week it is not for the reason that I have just mentioned. They want a shorter work week so that life may consist of something else than their daily toil. I hope that the government may give a lead in this matter, and the printing bureau would be a good place to start; and soon, I hope.
I understand that some of these grievances about which I have been speaking are issues right at the present time, perchance tonight, over at the printing bureau, while we are discussing them here. I feel it is unfortunate that these labour-management relationships in a plant that belongs to the people of Canada should be handled, as they have been to a large extent, by order in council. That is not the best way to achieve the best in labour-management relations, and it is because it has been done that way, because there is this dissatisfaction at the bureau, that I feel it is necessary to raise these matters tonight. The forty hour week and the labour-management relationship are extremely important but perhaps they are more or less of a long run nature. The immediate sore spots are the uncertainty as to when overtime rates of pay start, and the reduction in the night differential from 25 per cent to 15 per cent. I would be most happy if the Secretary of State could answer these points satisfactorily.

I do not know whether or not I can answer them satisfactorily, but I can attempt to answer them. The hon. member is quite correct on the question of overtime. An employee is supposed to put in his day's work before his overtime begins. If he stays away from work in the morning for an hour or two hours, as the case may be, the rule is he must put in his time that day before his overtime begins. If he is called in ahead of time he gets his overtime that much earlier in the day. As to the night differential, it is quite true that formerly it was 25 per cent, but I understand that in ordinary trade circles it is only 15 per cent, and it has been reduced in accordance with prevailing rates. The question of the forty-hour week is under consideration at the present time, but at the moment I understand that efforts are being made to readjust wages in both Toronto and Montreal, and we are awaiting the result of those negotiations. Then I think we shall be in a position to make a move in the matter.

It seems to me that there is a mistaken impression that the Indian population in our country is steadily decreasing and that, with the passing of the years, the number will become iess and less. That is not so. There was a Jecided drop in the Indian population of this country, from the figure of approximately

subtopic: RENT CONTROL-CORRESPONDENCE WITH PREMIERS OF SASKATCHEWAN AND QUEBEC MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
Ottawa, November 9, 1949
Honourable Maurice Duplessis,
Premier of Quebec,
Quebec City.
My dear Premier:
On October 23, 1948, I wrote to you about rent control, confirming the intention of the federal government to ask parliament for powers to extend rental control for a further twelve months beyond March 31, 1949.
In that letter I pointed out that:
"The constitutionality of continuing federal rent control has already been questioned and is now before the courts. The federal government does not wish to do anything to prevent any province from making provisions to deal with the situation that would arise should continuing federal rent control be held invalid and is prepared not only to make available to any province federal rental administration with all available staff, but also, subject to parliamentary approval, to pay the cost of any provincial rental administration for one year."
An exchange of correspondence then took place between us, but your government did not avail itself of our offer. Similarly, no other province requested us to vacate the field of rent control in its favour. Newfoundland, when it joined Canada, retained its own system of rent control.
Accordingly legislation extending rent control to March 31, 1950, was introduced into parliament and received approval.
On Thursday last, November 3, I made a statement in the House of Commons outlining the government's intentions with respect to the further extension of rent control. My statement will be found at page 1433 of Hansard for November 3.
In that statement I said:
"The government has therefore decided to refer the question of the validity of the rental regulations to the supreme court, in the hope and expectation that a decision will be given before the present legislation expires. As I have said, the law officers of the crown are of opinion that the rentals regulations are valid. They are also of opinion that both the law and the facts support the view that it lies within the authority of parliament to extend these regulations for a further period. Counsel will be instructed by the Attorney General of Canada to press this view before the court. The order in council making the reference is being prepared and when approved will be tabled in this house.
If no unfavourable decision is given, the government at the next session will ask parliament to grant a further extension of the rentals regulations. The government intends to continue with its program of orderly decontrol as rapidly as conditions warrant, but we do not believe that this program can be completed before March 31, 1950. Let me make it quite clear that the purpose of clarifying the legal position is not to perpetuate federal rent control. On the contrary, the purpose is to confirm our authority to proceed in an orderly way towards the eventual withdrawal of all controls. This has been our firm policy towards wartime controls in general and rent control is no exception.
Should the supreme court find that the rentals regulations are now beyond the powers of parliament, then of course a different situation arises. I am accordingly writing at once to the premiers of the provinces acquainting them with our intention and offering to assist in the preparation of what might be termed "stand-by" legislation if they wish to present such legislation to their respective legislatures.
After the most careful consideration of all the alternatives, the government believes that this course of action is the best. We believe that gradual and orderly decontrol is the right policy. At any time, however, that policy could be frustrated by an adverse decision of the courts. Such a decision might come at a most inconvenient time when the provinces might not be in a position to act as they see fit in the interests of their residents. By referring the question to the supreme court before the present legislation expires and by giving ample notice of our intention to do so, such a situation can, we hope, be avoided.
I should add that the federal government, of course, continues to stand ready at any time to vacate the field of rent control to any province which makes a formal request to that effect. We do not wish to stand in the way of any province which desires to operate in the field of rent control."
My purpose in writing to you at this time is to draw your attention to this statement of government policy and to offer to assist you in the preparation of provincial rent control legislation. If you wish to avail yourself of this offer, I shall be pleased to arrange to have Mr. Owen Lobley, the rentals administrator, put himself at your disposal.
Yours very truly,
D. C. Abbott
OFFICE OF THE PRIME MINISTER Province of Quebec
Quebec, November 16, 1949
Hon. D. C. Abbott,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Mr. Minister of Finance:
At the first cabinet meeting held since November 10th instant, I communicated to my colleagues of the executive council your letter concerning federal rent control, dated November 9 and delivered at my office the next day.
Your letter obviously concerns only particular aspects of this important problem. We respect your attitude in the matter without approving it.
Our view is and has always been that rental matters, concerning civil property and our civil code, come under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. We are certain that if the rights of the provinces in this matter had been recognized by the federal authorities the situation would have been considerably improved.
For more than eight years the federal authorities have assumed, in this field, powers of an essentially provincial nature. As a result, the situation has become very complicated, and many orders and rulings of the federal rental board have been unfortunate. We are of opinion that had the federal

authorities from the beginning consulted the provinces and recognized their rights in this field, we would not today have to deplore an unfortunate situation giving rise to numerous and legitimate protests and causing regrettable confusion.
For more than eight years federal bodies have, in that matter, caused many difficulties and disturbances which could and should have been avoided. After all the harm has been done, after the federal authorities have decided everything and the situation has been bungled and worsened, you say that the province may have some rights. As for us, we consider, as we always have, that these rights are unquestionable.
Eight years after entering a provincial field, you express the desire to submit to the supreme court the question of the constitutionality of the federal action and, at the same time, you anticipate the judgment of the supreme court and complicate the problem if possible still more.
It seems to us obvious that at the approach of winter, when householders are faced with the heavy expense of providing for the heating of their houses, and climatic conditions add considerably to the difficulties, the time is ill chosen to impose additional charges and obligations on the people.
Without any desire to criticize, but simply in order to re-establish the facts, we are of opinion that the central government's persistence in controlling rents has brought about a situation for which that government is undoubtedly responsible and which adds considerably to the inherent difficulties of the problem.
Ottawa has never offered to restore to us the full exercise of the rights which it has assumed in this field: the offers made to us in this matter are conditional, restrictive and, in the end, subordinate to the decision of the federal authorities.
As we declared on several occasions, the present government of the province of Quebec has always been willing to assume its obligations as it has always wished to see the federal government assume its own.
During eight years many federal orders in council have been passed and many rulings issued concerning rental control. All those documents are in the possession of the Ottawa authorities. In our view, it would be proper that we be permitted to make ourselves acquainted with their terms so that we might obtain at first hand the necessary explanations and information.
We thank you for your offer to place at our disposal the services and advice of the federal rental administrator. Without questioning his good faith and sincerity, we must say that we have greater need, in order to familiarize ourselves with the matter, of obtaining the rulings themselves and the federal orders in council.
As soon as we shall have received these necessary documents and have been able to examine them, you may be assured that the Quebec government will without delay take the fairest and most appropriate steps in the circumstances.
Yours sincerely,
M. L. Duplessis

Ottawa, November 24, 1949 The Honourable M. L. Duplessis,
Premier of Quebec,
Quebec, P.Q.
My dear Premier:
I acknowledge and thank you for your letter of November 16, in reply to mine of November 9, regarding rent control.
May I first comment on one or two of the points raised in your letter.
More than a year ago the federal government offered to vacate the field of rent control to any
Appendix
province which wished to introduce provincial legislation. In my letter to you of October 23, 1948, which contained that offer, I said:
"At the same time the federal government is prepared to vacate the field at any time after March 31, 1949, to any province which may decid to undertake rent control. Normally rent control would come under provincial jurisdiction and is peculiarly suitable for provincial or local administration because of the immovable nature of real property. The federal government is anxious not to stand in the way of any province which believes that rent control can be better undertaken and administered locally.
"This announcement of policy is being made at this time so that any provincial government which wishes to do so will have sufficient time to prepare legislation for presentation to its legislature before March 31, 1949."
Again, in a letter to me on November 3, 1948, you asked the following question:
"Does this mean that after March 31, 1949, you will definitely recognize the right and power of the province to establish, or not establish, as provincial authorities judge best, a provincial control on rentals? In other words, after March 31, 1949, will the federal government give the province exclusive power in these matters?"
On November 12, 1948, I replied to this question as follows:
"The government's policy, as announced, is that if after March 31, 1949, under the proposed extension of rent control, any provincial government formally requests that federal rental control be withdrawn in that province, the federal government will announce that it has received such a request and proceed to withdraw its controls at a date to be fixed by the provincial government in the light of the legislative plans of the province. The responsibility for rental control in that province will then rest with the provincial government and legislature."
As you will see, our offer was unconditional, without any qualification whatsoever. I therefore find it difficult to understand the statement in your letter of November 16, 1949, that:
"Ottawa has never offered to restore to us the full exercise of the rights which it has assumed in this field; the offers made to us in this matter are conditional, restrictive and, in the end, subordinate to the decision of the federal authorities." The federal authorities entered the field of rent control as part of a national policy of controlling prices and wages during wartime. It is generally agreed, I believe, that action on a national basis was in the general interest and essential to the successful conduct of the war. The government has been removing these controls gradually, as it announced it would, and as, indeed, it was bound to do. Broadly speaking, only rent control now remains, and this is also gradually being relaxed.
The reference to the supreme court is for the purpose of establishing whether or not the federal government has the authority to continue with this policy of gradual decontrol. At any time during the past year, however, any provincial government could have requested the federal government to vacate the field of rent control so as to leave that province free to enact its own legislation.
The federal government does not venture to suggest whether or not any province should enter the field of rent control. This is a matter which must be decided by the government and legislature of each province in the light of local circumstances. We have tried, however, to avoid standing in the way of any province which decides to do so.
The province of Newfoundland retained rent control on a provincial basis at time of union. Within the past few days I have also received a letter from

Appendix
Premier T. C. Douglas, of Saskatchewan, stating that it is the intention of the Saskatchewan government to enact rent control legislation in that province, to become effective on April 1, 1950. I have replied to Premier Douglas that the federal government is prepared to withdraw its regulations in Saskatchewan as of March 31, 1950, so as to avoid any possible conflict, and, if it is his wish, to suspend the operation of orders 813 and 814-which make provision for the recently announced changes in maximum rentals-in Saskatchewan so that the status quo will be retained in that province until provincial legislation comes into effect.
You ask for copies of our rent control regulations to assist you in reaching a decision on the matter. I have pleasure in forwarding, under separate cover, copies of all the orders, at present unrevoked, made in relation to rent control.
Yours very truly,
D. C. Abbott

Such a decision might come at a most inconvenient time when the provinces might not be in a position to act as they see fit in the interests of their residents. By referring the question to the supreme court before the present legislation expires and by giving ample notice of our intention to do so, such a situation can, we hope, be avoided.
I should add that the federal government, of course, continues to stand ready at any time to vacate the field of rent control to any province which makes a formal request to that effect. We do not wish to stand in the way of any province which desires to operate in the field of rent control."
My purpose in writing to you at this time is to draw your attention to this statement of government policy and to offer to assist you in the preparation of provincial rent control legislation. If you wish to avail yourself of this offer, I shall be pleased to arrange to have Mr. Owen Lobley, the rentals administrator, put himself at your disposal.
Yours very truly,
D. C. Abbott
PREMIER'S OFFICE Saskatchewan
Regina, November 16, 1949 The Honourable Douglas C. Abbott,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Abbott:
Re: Rent control
This will acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 9th instant.
I may say that the Saskatchewan government still holds the opinion expressed in my letter to you of January 28, 1949, that the dominion government should continue to exercise jurisdiction in the field of rent control. Dominion-wide control allows uniformity and other advantages. However, in view of the recent increases that you have announced, we are now of the opinion that if left in this type of dominion control, there will be no effective rent control. Further, you made the statement that:
"The government intends to continue with its program of orderly decontrol as rapidly as conditions warrant, but we do not believe that this program can be completed before March 31, 1950."

This confirms our belief that while your government intends, if jurisdictionally possible, to stay in the field, it will be in name only. The Saskatchewan government is gravely concerned with this problem, and feels that as long as there is as critical a shortage of housing as there is today, with the resultant grave injustice incurred by the people of this province, equitable rent control is a necessity.
We, therefore, believe that rental control should continue; we further believe that it would be most effective if dominion-wide, but as stated, we must express our dissatisfaction with the type of control that your government has indicated it intends to exercise. The government of Saskatchewan is, therefore, willing to accept the responsibility forced upon it and enter the field of rental control. It can, however, do this only if it has the assurance that its legislation will not be declared invalid by the Supreme Court of Canada. The law officers of the crown in Saskatchewan are not at all certain that either you, as the minister in charge, or the federal cabinet, has the power to carry out the offer made in your letter, and I quote:
"I should add that the federal government, of course, continues to stand ready at any time to vacate the field of rent control to any province which makes a formal request to that effect. We do not wish to stand in the way of any province which desires to operate in the field of rent control."
You can perhaps rescind all rent regulations in respect of Saskatchewan, and you can apparently, by order in council, vacate the field entirely. That is dominion-wide, but you do not appear to have authority to confer legislative jurisdiction on one province simply by executive action in rescinding regulations and orders respecting that province.
As a reference is being submitted to the supreme court, I would strongly urge your government to include in that reference a question that will settle this issue of power in yourself or the governor in council to confer legislative jurisdiction on a province by executive action designed to turn rent control over to that province.
It would seem that as long as the dominion has its present emergency legislation on the statute books, any single province, or any number of provinces less than all, is barred from the field.
In the tentative opinion our law officers have given, they have not overlooked the following provisions:
"4. The governor in council may revoke in whole or in part any order or regulation continued in force by or made under this act."
"3. (4) Every order made pursuant to the powers conferred by these regulations shall apply throughout Canada unless otherwise provided therein, but may apply to such area or areas in Canada or to such class or classes of persons or to such type or types of real property as such order may designate."
If, of course, the supreme court holds that jurisdiction lies in the provinces, none of these considerations will arise.
I would further strongly urge that until these matters have been settled, your government should rescind the recent increases announced and retain the status quo while these questions are being decided.
The Saskatchewan government, therefore, provided that this assurance of jurisdictional legality is given, would be prepared to enter the field of rent control. While we are at present preparing stand-by legislation, and while it would take some

Yours sincerely,
T. C. Douglas MINISTER OF FINANCE
Ottawa, November 23, 1949 The Honourable T. C. Douglas,
Premier of Saskatchewan,
Regina, Saskatchewan.
My dear Premier:
I wish to thank you for your prompt reply to my letter of November 9 regarding the future of rent control.
While the federal government has always believed that its wartime rent controls could not, and should not, be continued indefinitely, it recognized that some provinces might wish to enact measures of provincial rent control under the authority of section 92 of the British North America Act. For that reason the federal government, more than a year ago, offered to vacate the field in any province which wished to introduce its own legislation. This offer, as you know, was repeated again in my statement in the House of Commons on November 3.
You have now stated your intention to introduce legislation in Saskatchewan which will be effective as from April 1, 1950. The federal regulations are accordingly being amended to make them inoperative in Saskatchewan after March 31, 1950-or at an earlier date if that is your wish. There can then be no possible conflict between provincial and federal rental regulations in Saskatchewan, for ours will simply cease to be operative in that province. I am advised that there is no reasonable doubt regarding this point and that a reference to the supreme court is unnecessary.
You also asked that the recent amendments to the regulations which I announced on November 3 be suspended, pending clarification of the legal position and of the introduction by Saskatchewan of rent control legislation. As I have said, any doubt about the legal position seems to be without foundation. The federal government is, however, willing to amend orders 813 and 814 of the wartime prices and trade board, which provide for the changes recently announced, so as to make them inoperative in Saskatchewan. The status quo will therefore be maintained in Saskatchewan until provincial legislation comes into effect on or before April 1, 1950. You will understand, however, that this action was possible only because of your request to us to vacate the field and will be concurrent with an amendment to the federal rent control regulations which revokes them in their entirety in Saskatchewan as of March 31, 1950.
In other words, the position will be similar to what it would have been if your province had acted at an earlier date and was ready to put this legislation into effect now, with this exception, of course, that the federal regulations as they apply to Saskatchewan will remain as they are at the present time, unaffected by the changes recently announced, until your own legislation supersedes them.
Unless I hear from you to the contrary before December 1, I shall assume that these arrangements are acceptable to you. May I repeat my assurance that officials of the rentals administration will be ready to assist in the preparation of your legislation, should you desire them to do so.
Yours very truly,
D. C. Abbott
Saturday, November 26, 1949
